metadata.title: Prognostic Value of Vestibular Symptoms on the Vestibular Ocular Motor Screening for Return-to-play After Sport-related Concussion: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: The vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) contributes to gaze stabilization after head movement, but its independent prognostic value for return-to-play (RTP) after sport-related concussion (SRC) is unclear. This systematic review and meta-analysis examined associations between early vestibular-ocular motor screening (VOMS) assessment and RTP duration following SRC. METHODS: Searches of PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, PEDro, and Cochrane Library to March 2025 identified studies assessing within 14 days of SRC and reporting RTP outcomes. Two reviewers extracted data and assessed the risk of bias. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed for studies reporting prolonged recovery (≥28-30 days). RESULTS: Twelve studies (N = 3297 athletes) met inclusion criteria. Meta-analysis of four studies (n = 968) found a positive VOMS screen was associated with increased odds of prolonged recovery (odds ratio 2.39; 95% confidence interval, 1.82-3.13; P < 0.00001; I2=0%). Among nine studies of isolated VOR gain, eight reported significant univariate associations with longer RTP, but only two retained significance after multivariable adjustment. VOMS reliably identifies athletes at risk for protracted recovery, but isolated VOR measures show inconsistent independent predictive value after adjustment. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS: Objective VOR gain quantification (eg, vHIT, caloric) is needed to clarify whether physiological VOR dysfunction independently affects recovery. Clinicians should interpret VOR findings within a multimodal assessment.

metadata.title: Sex-related differences after ACL reconstruction differ between early functional recovery and 5-year outcomes.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: To compare early functional recovery and 5-year clinical, sports and psychological outcomes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) according to sex. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included consecutive patients who underwent primary ACLR between January 2017 and December 2019, with standardized 6-month functional and psychological assessment and available 5-year follow-up. Patients were analyzed according to sex. Baseline characteristics, 6-month quadriceps strength and hop-test performance, and 5-year patient-reported and sports outcomes were compared between groups. The primary outcome was recovery of preinjury activity level at 5 years, defined as a post-operative Tegner score greater than or equal to the preoperative Tegner score. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors independently associated with the primary outcome. RESULTS: A total of 479 patients were included, comprising 173 women (36.1%) and 306 men (63.9%). At 6 months, men demonstrated higher quadriceps limb symmetry and lower hop-test deficits than women, whereas anterior cruciate ligament return to sport after injury (ACL-RSI) did not differ significantly between groups. At 5 years, overall return-to-sport rates were similar between sexes (187 [61.2%] men vs. 103 [59.5%] women, p = 0.85), but men had higher post-operative Tegner (6 [5-7] vs. 5 [4-7], p < 0.001), IKDC (82.5 [75.7-87.3] vs. 79.5 [72.8-86.3], p = 0.02) and ACL-RSI scores (77.5 [55.8-92.5] vs. 69.2 [53.3-85.8], p = 0.02) and were more likely to recover their preinjury activity level (137 [45.1%] vs. 48 [28.1%], p < 0.001). In the baseline-adjusted multivariable model, male sex was independently associated with recovery of preinjury activity level (odds ratio [OR] = 2.16, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.40-3.39; p < 0.001). This association persisted after inclusion of 6-month recovery variables (OR = 1.93, 95% CI = 1.20-3.15; p = 0.007), while lower single-hop deficit was also independently associated with the outcome. CONCLUSIONS: Men and women did not demonstrate the same recovery profile after ACLR. Early differences were mainly functional, whereas 5-year differences involved recovery of preinjury activity level, subjective knee function and psychological readiness, despite similar overall return-to-sport rates. These findings suggest that return to sport should not be interpreted as equivalent recovery quality after ACLR. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

metadata.title: Low graft failure after primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in professional soccer players: A retrospective cohort study of 232 knees from the SANTI Study Group.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: This study aimed to determine graft failure rates after primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) in professional soccer players and to evaluate factors associated with graft failure, including lateral extra-articular augmentation. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study included 232 primary ACLRs in 215 professional soccer players: isolated ACLR (n = 31) and ACLR combined with a lateral extra-articular procedure (LEAP) (n = 201). The primary endpoint was graft failure, defined as symptomatic rupture confirmed clinically and by imaging or revision surgery. Time-to-event analyses accounted for variable follow-up. Contralateral ACL injury was recorded descriptively. RESULTS: At a mean follow-up of 100 months, 13 graft failures occurred (5.6%). Unadjusted failure rates were lower in ACLR + LEAP versus isolated ACLR (4.5% vs. 12.9%), but survival analysis showed no significant difference (hazard ratio [HR] 2.48; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.49-9.87; p = 0.246). Multivariable Cox regression identified no independent predictors of graft failure. Mean time to graft failure was longer in the ACLR + LEAP group than in the isolated ACLR group (54.8 ± 52.0 vs. 36.6 ± 38.2 months). Reoperations occurred in 32 knees (17.7%), with rates of 15.2% in the ACLR + LEAP group and 30.0% in the isolated ACLR group (p = 0.0528). Increased preoperative laxity (≥7 mm; HR 2.72; 95% CI 1.23-6.17; p = 0.014) and bone-patellar tendon-bone graft use (HR 3.14; 95% CI 1.26-7.20; p = 0.037) were independent risk factors for reoperation. Contralateral ACL injury occurred in 27.1% of knees, more frequently in female athletes (48.7% vs. 22.8%). Among patients who experienced graft failure, 53.8% also had a contralateral ACL injury. CONCLUSION: Primary ACL reconstruction in professional soccer players was associated with durable long-term graft survival. Although ACLR combined with an LEAP was associated with fewer graft failures than isolated ACLR, an independent protective effect was not confirmed. The high rate of contralateral ACL injury highlights the multifactorial nature of reinjury risk in this elite population. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective cohort study.

metadata.title: Effects of blood flow restriction training in adult upper-limb musculoskeletal rehabilitation: A systematic review.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Blood flow restriction training (BFRT) has been proposed as a low-load rehabilitation strategy for symptomatic and postoperative upper-limb musculoskeletal conditions. This review evaluated the clinical effects, tolerability, and prescription characteristics of BFRT in adult upper-limb musculoskeletal rehabilitation. METHODS: This systematic review was registered in International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420261299726) and reported with reference to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020. CENTRAL/Cochrane Library, Embase via Ovid, MEDLINE/PubMed, Science Citation Index/Web of Science, and Scopus were searched without a start-date restriction before February 18, 2026; backward reference-list/citation checking was also used. Randomized trials, case series, and case reports were eligible. Findings were synthesized narratively because of heterogeneity, and studies were appraised using risk of bias 2 or design-appropriate Joanna Briggs Institute checklists. RESULTS: Twenty reports were included: 9 parallel-group randomized trials, 1 randomized crossover trial, 2 case series, and 8 case-report publications. Across the reports, 340 participants were enrolled or randomized and 326 contributed to the analyzed/treated clinical samples; 158 were men (48.5%) and 168 were women (51.5%). In a sham-controlled lateral elbow tendinopathy trial, BFRT resulted in a significantly greater reduction in 12-week pain (between-group difference -1.54, 95% confidence interval [CI] -2.89 to -0.18; P = .026) and patient-rated tennis elbow evaluation (PRTEE) (-15.23, 95% CI -23.57 to -6.90; P < .001). In patients with chronic lateral epicondylitis, PRTEE reduction (-24.20 ± 4.02 vs -15.60 ± 3.71; P = .001) and quick disabilities of the arm, shoulder and hand reduction (-12.83 ± 4.97 vs -7.51 ± 4.72; P = .025) were significantly greater with BFRT plus conventional therapy, whereas between-group pain and strength changes were not significant. In nonoperative distal-radius-fracture rehabilitation, mean activity-pain reduction was 4.0 versus 2.3 points (P = .03). In rotator-cuff tendinopathy, BFRT resulted in significantly greater biceps thickness (P = .002) and internal-rotation strength (P = .040). Conversely, a pragmatic elbow trial found no significant between-group difference in 12-month PRTEE (adjusted contrast + 4.32, 95% CI -9.17 to 17.81; P = .53). CONCLUSION: BFRT may be considered a low-load adjunct in adult upper-limb musculoskeletal rehabilitation settings, but it is not consistently superior to active rehabilitation for pain, strength, or function. Confidence remains limited by small samples, heterogeneous prescriptions and co-interventions, uncontrolled designs, and incomplete adverse-event ascertainment.

metadata.title: Clinical Pathway Management for Platelet-Rich Plasma Therapy in Kellgren-Lawrence Grade I and II Knee Osteoarthritis: A Prospective, Multicenter, Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Clinical outcomes after platelet-rich plasma (PRP) treatment for knee osteoarthritis are inconsistent, and some well-designed trials show no benefit. Whether a standardized multicomponent pathway improves outcomes relative to conventional PRP care is uncertain. PURPOSE: To compare the efficacy, safety, satisfaction, and costs of a standardized PRP pathway versus physician-directed conventional PRP care in Kellgren-Lawrence grade I and II knee osteoarthritis. STUDY DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial; Level of evidence, 1. METHODS: At 3 hospitals, 240 patients were randomized 1:1 to a standardized PRP clinical pathway (PRP-CP; n = 120) or physician-directed conventional PRP care (PRP-C; n = 120). PRP-CP combined standardized selection, quality-controlled leukocyte-poor PRP, ultrasound-guided injections, staged rehabilitation, and systematic follow-up. Primary 12-month outcomes were visual analog scale (VAS) pain, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) total, and International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) scores; secondary outcomes included achievement of the minimal clinically important difference, satisfaction, adverse events, and costs. RESULTS: At 12 months, PRP-CP produced greater changes than PRP-C in VAS (mean difference [MD], -2.98 [95% CI, -3.64 to -2.32]), WOMAC total (MD, -8.63 [95% CI, -11.35 to -5.90]), and IKDC (MD, 10.25 [95% CI, 8.37 to 12.13]) scores (all P < .001). Achievement of the minimal clinically important difference favored PRP-CP at 3, 6, and 12 months for the VAS and at 6 and 12 months for the IKDC and WOMAC (P < .05). Satisfaction was greater with PRP-CP (odds ratio, 1.79 [95% CI, 1.11-2.89]; P = .017). An adverse event occurred in 17 of 115 patients in the PRP-CP group (14.8%) versus 36 of 113 patients in the PRP-C group (31.9%) (Fisher exact test: P = .003). Mean costs were CN¥15,199.9 versus CN¥14,754.4, respectively; the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was CN¥66.0 per WOMAC point. Effects were generally consistent across centers, and blinding was maintained. CONCLUSION: The standardized multicomponent pathway produced greater 12-month improvements in pain and function than conventional PRP care, with fewer adverse events. Because components were bundled and no placebo group was included, the trial does not establish PRP efficacy or component-specific effects.

metadata.title: Immobilisation versus early active motion following primary flexor pollicis longus tendon zones 1-2 repair: protocol for a registry-based multicentre randomised controlled trial in Sweden.
metadata.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Flexor pollicis longus (FPL) tendon injuries in the thumb are surgically challenging and require careful postoperative rehabilitation to avoid complications such as tendon rupture, stiffness and impaired hand function. Rupture rates after FPL repairs are substantially higher than those reported for finger flexor tendons. Although controlled early active motion (EAM) is widely used following FPL repairs, rehabilitation protocols developed for finger flexor tendons may not be directly transferable to the thumb because of differences in anatomy, biomechanics and functional demands. This study investigates whether immobilisation for 4 weeks postoperatively can reduce rupture rates without compromising functional outcomes after FPL injuries. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This registry-based randomised controlled unblinded superiority trial will be conducted across five academic hand surgery centres. Patients aged 15 years or older with a complete FPL injury in zone 1 or 2 will be included. Participants will be randomised 1:1 to either the EAM group, in which training starts 2–5 days postoperatively with protection by a dorsal cast and a volar removable splint or the casted immobilisation group for 4 weeks. After 4 weeks, the same rehabilitation protocol will be introduced for both groups. The primary outcome is the frequency of tendon rupture over 12 months. The secondary outcomes include patient-reported outcome measurements and patient-reported satisfaction, active range of motion of metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, grip and key pinch strength at 3 and 12 months postoperatively. All data are collected within the Swedish National Quality Registry for Hand Surgery. The primary outcome will be analysed on an intention-to-treat basis using a stratified analysis (stratified by centre), with the absolute risk difference and relative risk reported with 95% CIs. Secondary outcomes will be analysed using generalised estimating equations and standard tests for continuous and ordinal data, with results presented as effect estimates with 95% CI. ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: The trial was approved by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority (2025-00730-02). All participants are asked to provide written informed consent. The results will be disseminated as published articles in peer-reviewed journals. TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: NCT06836349.

metadata.title: Effectiveness of aerobic exercise on motor function and functional capacity in children and adolescents with neuromuscular diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate the effectiveness of aerobic exercise, alone or combined with other modalities, on motor function and functional capacity in children and adolescents with neuromuscular diseases (NMDs). MATERIALS AND METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted (CRD420251110784). Five databases were searched up to September 2025. Randomized and non-randomized trials assessing aerobic exercise in children/adolescents with NMDs were included. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were assessed using RoB2, ROBINS-I, and GRADE. Random-effects meta-analyses estimated standardized mean differences (SMD) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). RESULTS: Eleven studies (227 participants) were included. Aerobic exercise showed no significant effect on motor function (SMD = 0.15, 95% CI: -0.10 to 0.40, I2=0%) but produced moderate improvements in functional capacity (SMD = 0.51, 95% CI: 0.03 to 0.99, I2=78%). Subgroup analyses suggested non-significant effects for sessions <40 min (SMD = 0.83) and combined aerobic plus strength training (SMD = 0.74). Sensitivity analyses showed one study disproportionately influenced results; excluding high-risk studies yielded SMD = 0.36 (I2=0%). GRADE indicated low certainty for motor function and very low certainty for functional capacity. CONCLUSIONS: Aerobic exercise is safe and may improve functional capacity but not motor function in pediatric NMDs. Evidence is limited and needs for cautious interpretation and high-quality trials to inform clinical practice.

metadata.title: Comparison of short-foot and toe-curl exercises on movement control during single-leg landing after ACL reconstruction: An exploratory randomized controlled trial.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare the effects of short-foot exercise (SFE) and toe-curl exercise (TCE) on movement control during single-leg landing in individuals undergoing anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). DESIGN: Multicenter exploratory randomized controlled trial. SETTING: One hospital and two outpatient orthopedic clinics. PARTICIPANTS: Thirty-eight individuals who had undergone ACLR and demonstrated dynamic knee valgus during a single-leg landing task. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Participants were randomized to the SFE or TCE group, performed the allocated exercises daily, and received supervised exercise therapy once weekly for 12 weeks. The primary outcome was hip adduction excursion during single-leg landing. Assessments were conducted at baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks and analyzed using mixed models for repeated measures. RESULTS: At 6 weeks, hip adduction excursion was lower in the SFE group than in the TCE group, with a between-group difference of -6.30° (95% confidence interval [CI], -9.19 to -3.41; effect size [ES], -1.41). The between-group difference in change from baseline was -6.98° (95% CI, -9.88 to -4.08; ES, -1.57). At 12 weeks, hip adduction excursion remained lower in the SFE group. CONCLUSIONS: SFE may facilitate earlier improvement in frontal-plane movement control in patients who have undergone ACLR.

metadata.title: Acupuncture-Related interventions for exercise-induced delayed-onset muscle soreness in active adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis for sport rehabilitation.
metadata.abstract: BackgroundDelayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is a common post-exercise condition that can impair athletic performance, training quality, and rehabilitation.ObjectiveTo evaluate the efficacy and safety of acupuncture-related interventions for exercise-induced DOMS in active adults.MethodsPubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and CNKI were searched from inception to December 2025, with a manual reference-list update in January 2026. Randomized controlled trials comparing acupuncture-related interventions with sham/placebo or no treatment in healthy adults with exercise-induced DOMS were eligible. Nine RCTs met the eligibility criteria, and seven contributed compatible pain data to meta-analysis. Two reviewers independently extracted data, assessed risk of bias using RoB 2, and rated evidence certainty with GRADE. Pain intensity on a 0-10 visual analogue scale was pooled using random-effects models.ResultsAcross seven RCTs, acupuncture-related interventions reduced DOMS pain at 24 h (MD -0.62, 95% CI -1.01 to -0.23), 48 h (MD -0.71, 95% CI -1.20 to -0.22), and 72 h (MD -0.84, 95% CI -1.35 to -0.32). Heterogeneity was low (I2 = 0%, 3%, and 23%, respectively). None of the pooled estimates reached commonly cited 1.0- or 1.3-point pain thresholds, and no DOMS-specific minimal clinically important difference has been established. Evidence certainty was moderate.ConclusionAcupuncture-related interventions may provide modest short-term reductions in DOMS pain, but their clinical importance remains uncertain. The evidence base is small and does not support dry-needling-specific conclusions. Larger, rigorously controlled, modality-specific RCTs are needed.

metadata.title: Efficacy and safety study of diclofenac epolamine topical patch in accelerating rehabilitation of moderate hamstring strain: A randomized controlled trial.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Moderate hamstring strain is a common sports injury impairing daily and athletic function. While topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) offer localized pain relief with reduced systemic effects, high-quality evidence specific to hamstring injury is limited. OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the effect of a short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch combined with rehabilitation on pain and functional recovery in moderate hamstring strain. METHODS: In this single-center, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 patients were randomized to an experimental group (diclofenac patch twice daily for 14 days plus rehabilitation) or a control group (placebo patch plus identical rehabilitation). Outcomes assessed included pain measured by the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), as the primary endpoint, muscle strength, knee range of motion (ROM), functional back-kick test, time to rehabilitation criteria and safety (adverse events, liver/renal function). RESULTS: The diclofenac group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction at days 14, 21 and 28 post-intervention (all p < 0.01). Muscle strength recovery was superior at days 21 and 28, knee ROM improved more at day 28 and functional back-kick performance was better at day 28 (all p < 0.05). Time to meet rehabilitation criteria was significantly shorter in the experimental group (p = 0.002). Adverse event incidence and changes in liver/renal function were similar between groups (all p > 0.05). CONCLUSION: A short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch, combined with rehabilitation training, effectively alleviates pain, accelerates functional recovery, and is safe for treating moderate hamstring strain, supporting its use in clinical and sports rehabilitation.

metadata.title: Exercise, Medicine and Icing (EMI) for the Knee: Small Instalments, Big Gains in Early Osteoarthritis.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Early knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a common cause of pain and functional limitation, often managed conservatively with medications and physiotherapy. The EMI protocol (Exercise, Medicine, and Icing) was developed as a surgeon-led, home-based intervention aimed at improving pain, function, and muscle strength in patients with early knee OA. METHODS: This prospective, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial included 150 patients aged 40-70 years with Kellgren-Lawrence Grade 1-2 knee OA. Participants were randomised to receive either the EMI protocol (exercise, icing, and a standardised 6 week medical regimen including vitamin D, calcium, and magnesium supplementation) or the same medical regimen alone. The primary outcome was change in Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain score at 6 weeks. Secondary outcomes included Kujala score, quadriceps strength (manual muscle testing), rescue NSAID use, adherence, and adverse events over 1 year. RESULTS: At 1 year follow-up, 138 patients (92%) completed the study. The EMI group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction (VAS 6.6 ± 1.1-1.9 ± 0.9) compared with Medicine Alone (6.5 ± 1.2-3.4 ± 1.2; p < 0.001). Functional outcomes (Kujala score), quadriceps strength, and reduction in rescue NSAID use were also significantly superior in the EMI group. Adherence to exercise and icing was high, and adverse events were minimal and comparable between groups. CONCLUSION: The EMI protocol was associated with significantly greater improvements in pain, function, and quadriceps strength compared with medical therapy alone in patients with early knee OA. The findings support the incorporation of structured home-based exercise and cryotherapy into conservative management strategies for early knee OA. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s43465-026-01939-3.

metadata.title: Comparative efficacy of ultrasound-guided intra-articular injection of platelet-rich plasma (PRP), hydrolyzed type I collagen, and hyaluronic acid in patients with knee osteoarthritis: a randomized controlled trial.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intra-articular therapies are widely used for knee osteoarthritis (KOA), but direct comparisons between emerging biomaterials such as hydrolyzed collagen (HC) and established options like platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and hyaluronic acid (HA) are limited. OBJECTIVE: To compare the efficacy of intra-articular PRP, HC, and HA on pain, stiffness, and functional outcomes in KOA. METHODS: In this randomized, assessor- and statistician-blinded trial, 135 patients with Kellgren-Lawrence grade 2-3 KOA were assigned (1:1:1) to receive three ultrasound-guided Intra-articular injections of PRP, HC, or HA at two-week intervals. The primary outcome was change in WOMAC total score at 6 months. Secondary outcomes included WOMAC subscales, VAS pain, and the Lequesne Index. RESULTS: One hundred twenty-six patients completed follow-up. All groups showed significant improvements (p < 0.001). HA demonstrated greater improvements in some outcome measures at 1 month. PRP and HC demonstrated more sustained improvements than HA during 1 to 6 months follow-ups, although statistically significant between-group differences were limited to selected outcomes. No serious adverse events occurred. CONCLUSION: Intra-articular PRP, HC, and HA improved outcomes in mild to moderate knee OA; PRP and HC showed a trend toward more sustained benefits during 1 to 6 months. Longer-term trials are necessary to confirm these findings.

metadata.title: Non-Surgical Therapies for Knee Osteoarthritis: Current Evidence and Emerging Strategies.
metadata.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a degenerative joint disease characterized by pain, stiffness, and functional impairment. As many patients seek to avoid surgery, a synthesis of conservative treatment options is clinically relevant for evidence-based management. METHODS: A structured PubMed literature search was conducted through December 15, 2025. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials, cohort and case-control studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses evaluating nonsurgical interventions for knee OA. Extracted outcomes included pain, function, safety, and comparative effectiveness across reported follow-up durations. RESULTS: Intra-articular hyaluronic acid (HA) has a favorable safety profile and may delay progression to total knee arthroplasty, though benefits over placebo are modest and guideline recommendations inconsistent. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) improves pain and function and may outperform HA, although outcomes vary with preparation methods and study quality. Autologous conditioned serum and dextrose prolotherapy demonstrate symptomatic benefit, whereas corticosteroid injections primarily provide short-term relief. Disease-modifying osteoarthritis drugs (DMOADs), including sprifermin, lorecivivint, LNA043, cathepsin-K inhibition, ADAMTS-5 inhibition, and repurposed metabolic agents such as metformin, are emerging investigational strategies with variable structural and symptomatic results. Early evidence suggests mesenchymal stem cell-based therapies may improve outcomes but remain investigational. Core conservative measures, including exercise therapy, physical therapy, and weight reduction, consistently reduce pain and improve function. Assistive devices and valgus bracing provide additional symptomatic and biomechanical benefit. Among device-based interventions, cooled radiofrequency ablation offers durable pain relief compared with HA or corticosteroids, while sustained acoustic medicine and extracorporeal shockwave therapy show functional improvement; evidence for pulsed electromagnetic field therapy is mixed. Topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs provide effective analgesia with reduced systemic risk. CONCLUSION: Non-surgical management of knee OA should follow a stepwise approach, with rehabilitation and weight optimization as first-line therapy, selective injection- and device-based options for persistent symptoms, and timely surgical referral when disability remains refractory. Future progress will depend on standardized protocols and higher-quality long-term comparative trials to improve treatment selection and disease modification.

metadata.title: Selective recovery effects of short-term beetroot juice supplementation after exercise-induced muscle damage in trained female volleyball players.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Beetroot juice (BRJ) has been proposed as a nutritional aid for recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD), but evidence in female team-sport athletes is limited. It also remains unclear whether any benefit extends across functional, pain-related, swelling, and strength outcomes. METHODS: Seventeen female university volleyball players entered a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Four did not complete the second period, so outcomes were analyzed with linear mixed models. After baseline testing, participants performed 200 loaded vertical jumps and consumed BRJ or placebo at 24, 48, and 72 h post-EIMD. Recovery outcomes were countermovement jump (CMJ) height, volleyball-specific agility time, pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, visual analog scale soreness, and knee isokinetic measures. Holm-adjusted planned contrasts were used. RESULTS: CMJ height was the clearest BRJ-related functional finding. The treatment × time interaction showed a trend toward statistical significance (P = 0.062), and CMJ height was higher under BRJ than PLA at 72 h post-EIMD (P = 0.033, d = 1.01). Calf pressure pain threshold also favored BRJ at 72 h, accompanied by a significant treatment × time interaction (P < 0.001). In contrast, agility time and soreness changed over time without clear between-condition differences, while thigh pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, and low-velocity knee isokinetic outcomes showed no consistent BRJ-related advantage. CONCLUSIONS: Short-term BRJ supplementation was associated with selective rather than generalized recovery benefits after EIMD in trained female volleyball players. The clearest findings were higher CMJ height and calf PPT under BRJ than PLA at 72 h, whereas the remaining outcomes showed no consistent treatment-related differences.

metadata.title: Physical activity levels two years after total knee arthroplasty and preoperative patient characteristics: a secondary analysis of the MOVE randomized controlled trial.
metadata.abstract: INTRODUCTION: At one year after total knee arthroplasty (TKA), patients are less physically active than age-matched peers, but physical activity (PA) trajectories two years after TKA are unclear. This study examined PA levels from baseline to two years post-TKA, quantified return to baseline PA levels over time, and evaluated associations between baseline participant characteristics and post-TKA PA levels. METHODS: This was an exploratory secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial. Participants (n = 135) aged 50 to 85 years undergoing primary unilateral TKA wore accelerometers preoperatively and 10 weeks, six months, and two years post-TKA to characterize light PA, moderate-vigorous PA (MVPA), and steps/day. Descriptive statistics were used to characterize PA levels. Repeated measures models estimated PA levels over time. The percentage of participants who returned to or exceeded baseline PA levels over time was quantified. Multivariate logistic regressions modeled return to baseline PA levels over time to evaluate associations with baseline participant characteristics. All models controlled for age, sex, and treatment group. RESULTS: There was an increase of 8% steps/day and 0.75% MVPA from baseline to two years post-TKA. At two years post-TKA, 54.2, 53.1, and 55.6% of participants returned to baseline light PA, MVPA, and steps/day levels. Higher baseline PA levels were associated with lower odds of returning to baseline levels at all timepoints for MVPA (10 weeks odds ratio (95% confidence interval): 0.62 (0.46 to 0.84); six months: 0.55 (0.40 to 0.76); two years: 0.52 (0.36 to 0.75)), as well as light PA and steps/day (all P-values < 0.05). Baseline body mass index, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index scores, and Functional Comorbidity Index were associated inconsistently with PA levels. CONCLUSION: While on average, PA levels increased from baseline to two years post-TKA, participants who have higher baseline PA levels had reduced odds of returning to the same level. These findings suggest TKA and current rehabilitation may not fully address PA, and additional support (e.g., behavioral guidance or tailored rehabilitation) may be needed.

metadata.title: Clinical and functional outcomes of aquatic plyometrics in adolescent patellofemoral pain syndrome: a dual-arm randomized controlled trial.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Optimal management of adolescent patellofemoral pain syndrome requires evidence-based interventions that maximize physical recovery without overloading the patellofemoral joint. This study investigated the efficacy of aquatic plyometric (Aquatic-Plyo) exercises on pain, muscle strength, and functional disability and health-related quality of life in this demographic. DESIGN: A dual-arm randomized controlled trial. SUBJECTS/PATIENTS: 56 adolescents with patellofemoral pain syndrome (age: 10-18 years). METHODS: Adolescents were allocated to an experimental Aquatic-Plyo group or a control group performing conventional exercises. Both arms completed 45-min sessions twice weekly for 12 weeks. Pre- and post-treatment assessments included pain intensity, isokinetic knee (quadriceps and hamstrings) torque at 120°/s and 180°/s, functional disability, and health-related quality of life. RESULTS: Mixed-model ANOVA confirmed the therapeutic dominance of the Aquatic-Plyo protocol. It yielded superior pain relief (p = 0.004, η2p = 0.14) and larger increases in quadriceps [120°/s (p = 0.006, η2p = 0.13); 180°/s (p = 0.008, η2p = 0.12)] and hamstring [120°/s (p = 0.007, η2p = 0.13); 180°/s (p = 0.023, η2p = 0.09)] peak torque. Moreover, the Aquatic-Plyo intervention drove greater reduction in functional disability (p = 0.03, η2p = 0.08) and notable enhancement in perceived health-related quality of life (p = 0.023, η2p = 0.09). CONCLUSION: Aquatic-Plyo exercises effectively reduces pain and disability while improving muscle strength and health-related quality of life in adolescents with patellofemoral pain syndrome, making it a valuable addition to conservative rehabilitation strategies.

metadata.title: Conservative Management of a Displaced Iliopsoas Avulsion in an Adolescent: A Case Report and Systematic Review.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To report a case of traumatic iliopsoas tendon avulsion with displacement exceeding the commonly cited 2-cm surgical threshold, managed successfully without surgery, and to systematically review the literature on optimal treatment and return-to-sport outcomes. DESIGN: Case report combined with a PRISMA-compliant systematic review of PubMed, Cochrane Library, and Embase. SETTING: Level I university trauma center; systematic review of published case reports and series. PARTICIPANTS: A 16-year-old male competitive soccer player (index case) and 58 additional patients from the literature, predominantly adolescent males with sports-related iliopsoas avulsion. INTERVENTIONS: The index patient received conservative treatment with staged weight bearing and structured physiotherapy. Across the literature, 90% (52/58) were treated conservatively and 10% operatively. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Clinical recovery, strength restoration, radiographic union on MRI, and return to sport. RESULTS: Eighteen studies (58 patients; 59 including this case) were analyzed. A bony lesser-trochanter avulsion was present in 98% (57/58). Of at least 9 patients with displacement >2 cm, 5 recovered fully nonoperatively. The index patient was pain-free with full strength and unrestricted soccer return at 3 months; 6-month MRI showed radiographic nonunion despite complete functional recovery. Return to sport approached 100%, typically within 10 to 12 weeks. CONCLUSIONS: Available very low-certainty evidence suggests that nonoperative management can achieve favorable clinical recovery and return to sport after traumatic iliopsoas avulsion, including in some cases with displacement greater than 2 cm. Return-to-sport decisions may reasonably prioritize restored, pain-free function over radiographic union, but larger prospective studies are needed.

metadata.title: Effects of Whey Protein Supplementation on Muscle Damage, Hepatic Stress, and Inflammatory Markers in Power- and Endurance-Trained Athletes.
metadata.abstract: This study investigated the effects of 8 weeks of whey protein supplementation (30 g/day) on biomarkers of liver function, inflammation, and muscle damage in trained power-trained (predominantly speed-power/anaerobic-power disciplines) and endurance-trained athletes, in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Fifty-nine male athletes were stratified into power (n = 30) and endurance (n = 29) groups, then randomly assigned to a whey protein group (WG) or a placebo control group (CG). Biomarkers assessed pre- and post-intervention included alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), C-reactive protein (CRP), and creatine kinase (CK). Significant reductions in ALT, AST, and CK were observed in both endurance- and power-trained athletes after supplementation (p = 0.001, p = 0.015, p = 0.001, and p = 0.003 respectively), indicating attenuated hepatic and muscular stress. Among the four biomarkers, only ALT displayed a statistically significant three-way interaction (Time × Supplementation × Training modality; p = 0.003), identifying it as the sole marker showing a genuine modality-specific differential response to supplementation. A significant within-group reduction in CRP was additionally observed in the supplemented power-trained athletes (p = 0.039), whereas endurance athletes showed only minor, non-significant changes; because the omnibus three-way interaction for CRP was not significant, this finding is reported as a within-group trend rather than evidence of a differential effect between modalities. Placebo groups demonstrated stable or increased enzyme and CRP values, particularly in endurance athletes. These findings suggest that whey protein may attenuate exercise-induced hepatic and muscular stress across training modalities, with a modality-specific effect on hepatic stress markers (ALT) observed in power-trained athletes. The results highlight whey protein's potential as a nutritional aid to promote recovery and physiological adaptation, possibly mediated by antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms. Further studies are warranted to examine long-term outcomes and dose-response effects across different training profiles.

metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy of intra-articular orthobiologics versus standard active control (arthrocentesis or hyaluronic acid) on pain, mouth opening and structural bone gain in advanced degenerative temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disease, stratified by orthobiologic class and joint compartment. DESIGN: Systematic review with exploratory meta-analysis, following PRISMA and prospectively registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261425634), of RCTs published January 2020-June 2026. Outcomes were pooled as mean difference (MD) by orthobiologic class, with joint compartment as a three-level moderator. Clinical relevance was assessed against minimal important difference (MCID) thresholds; non-randomised studies were synthesised narratively. RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies were included: 18 RCTs (≈862 patients; 12 pooled) and 10 narrative studies. Versus hyaluronic acid, orthobiologics reduced pain (MD -0.71) and improved mouth opening (MD 3.04 mm), both below the MCID. Versus arthrocentesis alone, effects were larger: pain (MD -1.57, exceeding the MCID) and mouth opening (MD 3.46 mm, below the MCID), with high heterogeneity unexplained by orthobiologic class. No RCT tested the dual joint space approach, represented only by one narrative study. A subset of studies had incomplete degenerative anchoring or unreported compartment. Certainty of evidence was low to very low. CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence does not support a firm recommendation for any single orthobiologic in advanced degenerative TMJ disease, reinforcing a conservative, stepwise approach. Dual joint space therapy - a plausible but untested hypothesis - remains unstudied and is a priority for future research.

metadata.title: Cold-Water Immersion for Post-exercise Recovery: An Overlap-Aware Umbrella Review.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cold-water immersion (CWI) is widely used after strenuous exercise, but review-level findings vary by outcome, comparator, recovery window, population, and protocol. Reuse of the same primary studies across reviews can also exaggerate apparent consistency. METHODS: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, Cochrane Library, Embase, and Scopus from inception to 30 January 2026 for systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and network meta-analyses of post-exercise CWI. Fourteen reviews were included. Primary-study overlap was quantified using the corrected covered area (CCA) overall and for outcome-specific study-to-review mappings. Because overlap was high and review-level estimates were statistically dependent, we did not perform second-order meta-analysis. Source-verified estimates were synthesized in a structured, overlap-aware format. Methodological quality was assessed with AMSTAR 2. RESULTS: Of the 14 included reviews, 13 provided quantitative estimates, whereas one review provided narrative evidence on heart rate variability (HRV). Overall CCA was 12.68% (high); 99 of 165 primary-study families appeared in at least two reviews. Outcome-specific CCA was 15.03% for delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS; very high) and ranged from 0.00% for interleukin-6 (IL-6) to 25.00% for C-reactive protein (CRP). It was not calculable for HRV, because one review contributed. AMSTAR 2 confidence was low in 2 reviews and critically low in 12. DOMS showed the most consistent favorable pattern: source-review standardized mean differences ranged from -1.04 to -0.37, although the largest estimate was soccer-specific and its 95% prediction interval crossed zero. Because DOMS evidence was highly redundant across the contributing reviews, this apparent consistency does not represent independent replications. Findings for objective performance and biochemical outcomes were inconsistent, time-dependent, or comparator-dependent. CONCLUSIONS: Within the available review-level evidence, CWI was associated with the most consistent reduction in self-reported short-term post-exercise DOMS, but the clinical importance of the observed effects remains uncertain. Evidence does not support a uniform benefit across objective performance or inflammatory outcomes. Protocol observations, including commonly studied temperatures and durations, are descriptive and should not be interpreted as an optimized prescription. Trial Registration PROSPERO CRD420261332482.

metadata.title: Short-term Rhodiola rosea supplementation improves premenstrual symptoms, reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes: a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Premenstrual symptoms may negatively influence psychological readiness, cognitive-motor performance, and perceived exertion in female athletes. Rhodiola rosea (RR) is an adaptogenic herb that has been investigated for its potential effects on fatigue, stress tolerance, mood, and exercise-related outcomes. However, its effects on premenstrual symptoms and performance-related responses in female athletes remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase on premenstrual symptoms, peripheral serum serotonin and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) concentrations, reaction time, perceived exertion, and aerobic performance-related indices in female taekwondo athletes with premenstrual syndrome (PMS). METHODS: In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 24 female taekwondo athletes with moderate-to-severe PMS symptoms were randomly assigned to receive either 500 mg/day of standardised RR extract (n = 12) or placebo (n = 12) for 10 days during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase. Premenstrual symptoms were assessed using the Premenstrual Symptoms Screening Tool (PSST). Visual reaction time, peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations, time to exhaustion (TTE), estimated VO₂max, and rating of perceived exertion (RPE) were evaluated before and after the intervention. Data were analysed using analysis of covariance with baseline values as covariates. RESULTS: Compared with placebo, RR supplementation significantly reduced several PMS symptoms, including irritability, depression, anxiety, social withdrawal, decreased concentration, hypersomnia, food cravings, crying, skin problems, and abdominal pain (p < 0.05). The RR group demonstrated faster reaction time compared with placebo (adjusted mean difference: -60 ms; p < 0.001). Peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations were significantly higher in the RR group than in the placebo group (p < 0.001). In addition, RR supplementation reduced post-exercise RPE (adjusted mean difference: -1.40 Borg units; p = 0.006). However, no significant differences were observed between groups in TTE or estimated VO₂max (p > 0.05). CONCLUSION: Short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase may improve selected PMS symptoms, visual reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes with PMS. Larger trials with hormonal confirmation of menstrual cycle phase, longer intervention periods, direct physiological measurements, and sport-specific performance assessments are required to confirm these findings.

metadata.title: Orthobiologics for hand and wrist disorders: An indication-specific systematic review and evidence-gap synthesis.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Orthobiologics are increasingly used in hand and wrist disorders; however, their clinical effectiveness remains uncertain due to heterogeneity in indications, formulations, and outcome reporting. METHODS: This systematic review was reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261359867). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Web of Science were searched from inception through March 31, 2026. Primary clinical studies evaluating locally delivered orthobiologics for hand or wrist disorders were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 for randomized trials and ROBINS-I for nonrandomized comparative studies and the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist for uncontrolled case series; certainty was evaluated using GRADE. Because the studies differed substantially in indication, biologic formulation, comparator, follow-up, and outcome definition, meta-analysis was not clinically appropriate; a structured qualitative synthesis was performed. RESULTS: Ten primary clinical studies were included: three studies of carpal tunnel syndrome, one of de Quervain tenosynovitis, three of trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis, one of distal-radius fracture, and two of scaphoid nonunion. No meta-analysis was performed. Evidence for carpal tunnel syndrome was inconsistent across comparators and follow-up durations. In de Quervain tenosynovitis, PRP produced outcomes comparable to corticosteroid injection, with fewer reported local adverse effects. Evidence for trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis was limited and comparator-dependent. In scaphoid nonunion, the primary BMP studies suggested possible osteoinductive benefit but also identified complications, including heterotopic ossification, persistent nonunion, and reoperation. Overall certainty ranged from moderate to very low. CONCLUSIONS: Orthobiologic effectiveness for hand and wrist disorders appears indication-specific but is supported by limited and heterogeneous evidence. Routine PRP use in osteoarthritis is not supported, and application in other conditions should remain selective and context-dependent. Larger, adequately powered, placebo-controlled trials with standardized biologic characterization and outcome reporting are required. These findings should be interpreted as an evidence-gap map rather than proof of comparative efficacy. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV (systematic review of predominantly small randomized and nonrandomized studies with heterogeneous designs and limited sample sizes).

metadata.title: The longitudinal relationship between physical capacity and self-perceived physical functioning after total hip and knee arthroplasty.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To examine longitudinal within-person effects between capacity and self-perceived performance during postoperative physiotherapy in patients with total hip and knee arthroplasty (THA/TKA). METHODS: We performed a secondary analysis of a cluster randomized controlled trial on physiotherapy after THA and TKA using random intercept cross lagged panel models. Capacity was assessed with the 40-m fast-paced walk test (40 m FPWT) and the 30-s chair-stand test (30-s CST), and self-perceived performance with the Oxford Hip/Knee Score functioning subscale (OHS/OKS) and the Hip disability/Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score-Physical function Short form (HOOS-PS/KOOS-PS). Assessments were performed preoperatively and at 3 and 12 months postoperatively. RESULTS: 312 THA (mean age 66, SD: 9; 53% female) and 312 TKA (mean age 67, SD: 8; 55% female) were included. From pre-surgery to 3 months, no effects were found between capacity and self-perceived performance in either THA or TKA.From 3 to 12 months, in THA, 40 m FPWT performance at 3 months had a positive effect (β 0.34, 95% CI 0.05-0.63) on HOOS-PS scores at 12 months. In TKA, 40 m FPWT performance at 3 months had a positive effect on both OKS functioning (β 0.24 95% CI 0.05-0.43) and KOOS-PS (β 0.29 95% CI 0.11-0.47) scores at 12 months. No other effects were observed. CONCLUSION: From pre-surgery to 3 months, capacity and self-perceived performance showed no effects within individuals. However, during the early postoperative phase, gait speed may be a relevant treatment target to improve long-term self-perceived performance.

metadata.title: Additive effects of active vitamin D3 or vitamin E administration on therapeutic lower-limb home exercise for knee osteoarthritis: A pilot prospective randomized controlled trial.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Quadriceps weakness, inflammation, and reduced physical function are common in knee osteoarthritis (OA), and lower limb exercise therapy is an established non-pharmacological treatment. Vitamin D3 (vit D3) and vitamin E (vit E) have been proposed as adjunctive therapies; however, clinical findings are inconsistent. We aimed to examine whether combining lower limb home exercises with oral active vit D3 or vit E supplementation provides additive benefits compared with home exercise alone in women with symptomatic knee OA. METHODS: Eighty-eight postmenopausal women with knee OA (Kellgren-Lawrence grade 2-4; 71.9 ± 5.6 years) were randomly assigned to receive therapeutic lower limb home exercise only, home exercise with active vit D3 administration, or home exercise with vit E administration. Participants performed isometric lower limb exercises twice daily for 24 weeks. Subsequently, they were assessed using the Japanese knee osteoarthritis measure (JKOM) as the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes were short-form health survey, grip strength, quadriceps muscle strength, 10-m walk test, inflammatory markers, bone mineral density, and body composition. For data analyses, we used paired and independent t tests, analysis of variance, and analysis of covariance, adjusting for age, body mass index, and Kellgren-Lawrence grade. RESULTS: Eighty participants completed follow-up. All groups showed significant improvements in JKOM score, quadriceps muscle strength, and 10-m walk test. Grip strength improved significantly only in the group that received active vit D. No significant between-group differences were observed in JKOM scores, short-form health survey-36, muscle strength, or physical performance. Inflammatory markers decreased significantly in the vit E group, although between-group differences were not observed. No other significant between-group differences were found, except in bone mineral density. CONCLUSIONS: Administering active vit D3 or vit E for 24 weeks as an adjunct to lower limb home exercises did not yield significant additive effects on symptoms, muscle strength, or physical performance in women with knee OA. Exercise therapy alone remained effective, and vitamin supplementation showed nutrient-specific trends.

metadata.title: The Effect of Acute Beetroot Juice and Caffeine Supplementation on Specific Judo Performance During a Simulated Competition Day in Judo Athletes.
metadata.abstract: Beetroot juice (BJ) and caffeine (CAF) are well-established ergogenic aids for exercise performance. However, little is known about their efficacy and interaction within the specific context of a judo competition day. This study investigated the acute effects of BJ, CAF, and their combination (BJCAF) on judo-specific performance across a simulated competition day. Using a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover design, 35 competitive judo athletes (age 23 ± 5 years; body mass 74 ± 13 kg) completed 4 sessions (BJ, CAF, BJCAF, and placebo), each consisting of 5 trials of judo randori and a Special Judo Fitness Test (SJFT), followed by neuromuscular and cognitive assessments. Compared with placebo, CAF enhanced SJFT performance, neuromuscular function, and cognition in trials 1-3 but not in trial 5 (p < 0.05). Conversely, BJ improved these same metrics in trial 5 (p < 0.05). BJCAF enhanced SJFT performance across trials 1-3 and 5, cognitive functions in trials 1, 2, and 4, and neuromuscular performance in all trials (p < 0.05). Importantly, in trial 5, both BJ and BJCAF conditions yielded improved SJFT performance, neuromuscular function, and cognitive outcomes compared to CAF alone (p < 0.05). The results demonstrate that the ergogenic effect of CAF was not maintained throughout the simulated competition day, whereas BJ provided late-stage benefits. Co-ingestion effectively counteracted the later-session decline observed with CAF alone while maintaining its early advantages. This highlights the importance of considering temporal dynamics and metabolic costs when designing nutritional strategies for multi-bout, high-intensity sports tournaments such as judo.

metadata.title: Beyond the pump: a narrative review of the acute molecular, metabolic, and neuropsychological responses to a bout of resistance exercise.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Resistance training is widely recognized for its chronic adaptations, including strength, muscle hypertrophy, and improvements in musculoskeletal health. However, a single bout of resistance exercise also elicits a range of acute physiological and psychological responses across multiple systems. These immediate responses have generally been examined within individual physiological domains, with less attention given to their coexistence and temporal overlap following a single session. METHODS: This narrative review synthesizes evidence relating to the acute systemic effects of a single bout of resistance exercise. Literature was identified through iterative searches of electronic databases and reference lists, with emphasis on primary human studies directly examining acute responses, alongside relevant systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and mechanistic literature. RESULTS: Acute resistance exercise induces responses across endocrine and myokine, metabolic, vascular, pain-related, psychological, cognitive, and sleep-related domains. Contracting skeletal muscle releases myokines and other signalling molecules with potential systemic actions. Post-exercise energy expenditure and muscle protein synthesis may remain elevated during recovery, while glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity are enhanced. Acute resistance exercise can also produce exercise-induced hypoalgesia, reduce state anxiety, improve aspects of executive function and cognitive performance, and may influence sleep continuity and neurophysiological activity. These responses differ in their evidential basis and physiological significance, encompassing directly observed short-term effects, proposed regulatory mechanisms, and more tentative hypotheses regarding longer-term implications. CONCLUSION: A single bout of resistance exercise produces temporally overlapping responses across multiple physiological and psychological systems. These responses should not be assumed to represent adaptive remodelling or direct mechanisms of chronic health benefit. Nevertheless, integrating them provides a broader perspective on the immediate multisystem consequences of resistance exercise and may help inform future research examining how repeated acute responses relate to longer-term adaptation and health outcomes.

metadata.title: Effects of a chickpea protein hydrolysate on exercise-induced biomarkers of muscle damage and inflammation in federated road cyclists.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial examined the effects of a chickpea protein hydrolysate (CPH) on biomarkers associated with exercise-induced muscle damage and inflammation in federated male road cyclists. METHODS: Twenty-four participants completed a 14-day intervention receiving either 12 g/day of chickpea protein hydrolysate (EXP) or a placebo (PLA) following training sessions. The selected dose was based on previous studies demonstrating antioxidant and immunomodulatory bioactive properties of the hydrolysate. Nutritional intake and training were registered. Body composition and biochemical markers of muscle damage and inflammation were assessed before and after the study. RESULTS: No significant differences were observed in body composition, training load, or dietary intake between groups, indicating controlled experimental conditions. However, between-group analyses of change scores revealed significant differences for lactate dehydrogenase (LDH; p = 0.04) and C-reactive protein (CRP; p = 0.02), favoring the experimental group. LDH decreased in the EXP group while increasing slightly in the placebo group, whereas CRP decreased in EXP and increased in PLA. Although creatine kinase (CK) showed a favorable pattern in the EXP group, the between-group comparison did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.062). Myoglobin followed a similar downward trend. The high baseline protein intake (>2 g/kg/day) and short intervention duration may have limited changes in body composition, nevertheless, the observed biomarker responses suggest that CPH supplementation may influence selected physiological processes associated with exercise-induced inflammation and cellular stress. CONCLUSIONS: In trained cyclists with high habitual protein intakes, 14 days of CPH supplementation did not alter body composition but was associated with favorable changes in selected biomarkers related to exercise-induced inflammation and cellular stress compared with placebo. Given the short intervention period and the absence of direct assessments of recovery or performance, these findings should be interpreted as short-term biochemical responses. Further studies are required to determine their physiological relevance and whether these biomarker changes translate into meaningful improvements in recovery, training adaptation, or athletic performance.

metadata.title: Characterising the Internal and External Load During Warm-Up, Match Play and Training in Soccer Substitutes: A Systematic Scoping Review.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Shorter match-play exposure for soccer substitutes relative to those who start matches has implications in the days before, during and following match play concerning their training, preparatory and recovery/compensatory practices. Specifically, characterising the internal and external loading of substitute players throughout a weekly microcycle can facilitate evidence-based recommendations aimed at optimising their performance readiness. OBJECTIVES: This systematic scoping review aimed to map and characterise the internal and external loading associated with warm-up, match play and training in soccer substitutes. METHODS: Prior to literature searches being conducted, a Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Study design (PICOS) statement was formed. Online database (PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Scopus and Web of Science) searches were performed according to PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) protocols. Studies were eligible if internal or external characteristics of soccer substitutes were measured in training or match-play scenarios. After calibration exercises, two authors independently quality assessed each study, with Cohen's kappa undertaken to assess inter-rater agreement. A scoping review methodology was selected because of the methodological and conceptual heterogeneity across studies, which precluded meaningful meta-analysis. RESULTS: A total of 5135 studies were identified, 66 of which met study criteria. Substantive inter-rater agreement was observed (κ = 0.939, p < 0.001) during the quality assessment of included studies. Soccer substitutes' body temperature, and thus several aspects of physical performance, may not be maintained at time of pitch entry (body temperature pre-pitch entry ~ 37 °C vs match play > 38 °C). Substitutes may experience lower absolute physical loading during training and match day (e.g. match-day 'top up' activity: ~ 17 min; total distance: ~ 1700 m) but during match play, substitutes typically cover higher relative total distances (~ 109 to ~ 137 m·min-1), high-speed running (~ 9.8 to ~ 13.5 m·min-1) and sprinting distance (~ 3.8 to 5.0 m·min-1) compared with players who started the match. Substitutes playing in the second-half exhibit increased heart rates compared with full-match players (84% vs 81% maximum heart rate); however, this remains lower than the first-half heart rate responses of full-match players (84% vs 86% maximum heart rate). CONCLUSIONS: This systematic scoping review summarises current evidence and key findings relating to the internal and external characteristics of soccer substitutes during warm-up, match play and training that can be used in practice to inform player welfare and sport science support within these cohorts. Chiefly, during match-day warm-ups, soccer substitutes' body temperature and physical performance responses may not be maintained, despite typical substitute-specific match-day practices being employed. Similarly, soccer substitutes were frequently reported to demonstrate higher relative total distance, high-speed running and sprinting outputs compared with starting players. Further research is needed to better understand performance demands, longitudinal adaptations, contextual influences and female-specific responses in soccer substitutes.

metadata.title: Evolution of Reverse Shoulder Arthroplasty: Two Decades of Evidence from the Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Reverse shoulder arthroplasty (rTSA) has evolved from a salvage procedure to a widely adopted reconstructive solution. This study performed a descriptive bibliometric and content-trend analysis of rTSA publications in the Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery (JSES) from 2004-2025. METHODS: A systematic review identified 506 clinical rTSA studies published in JSES between 2004 and 2025. Extracted variables included publication year, level of evidence, authorship, institution, geographic origin, research topic, demographics, indications, complications, and implant characteristics. Temporal trends were tested using Mann-Kendall trend test and segmented regression; the relationship between implant design representation and complication reporting was evaluated with Spearman rank correlation. RESULTS: Annual publications increased significantly (BH-adjusted P < .001), peaking at 51 studies in 2023. Mean level of evidence improved (BH-adjusted P < .001), from 4.0 (2006) to 2.86 (2023). Early authorship centered on foundational surgeons (Frankle, Boileau, Walch) and European institutions, later diffusing globally. Mean age rose modestly, though this did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons (BH-adjusted P = .077), stabilizing near 70-72 years after 2012. Research focus shifted from complications/technique toward outcomes after 2013, then toward instrumentation, rehabilitation, and cost. Osteoarthritis indications increased (BH-adjusted P = .005) while revision surgery declined (BH-adjusted P = .002). Implant design shifted from medialized to lateralized/non-Grammont configurations (both BH-adjusted P < .001). No individual complication subtype showed a significant temporal trend. CONCLUSION: RTSA publication trends in JSES reflect the field's evolution from complication-focused study to evidence-driven refinement. Implant design, evidence level, and indications changed significantly, alongside, but not statistically linked to, complication reporting, informing future shoulder reconstruction research directions. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Literature Review, Bibliometric Analysis.

metadata.title: Quantitative UTE MRI Differences in the Meniscus Following ACL Reconstruction: A Prospective Cohort Study Using 3D Ultrashort Echo Time Adiabatic T1rho and Magnetization Transfer Imaging.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: ACLR is associated with altered joint loading and increased risk of post-traumatic osteoarthritis. Conventional MRI has limited sensitivity to early meniscal differences because of short-T2 signal decay and magic-angle effects. PURPOSE: To evaluate whether 3D ultrashort echo time imaging-based adiabatic T1rho (UTE-Adiab-T1rho) and ultrashort echo time imaging-based macromolecular fraction (UTE-MMF) identify regional quantitative MRI differences after ACLR. STUDY TYPE: Prospective longitudinal cohort study. POPULATION: 30 control scans, 19 ACLR scans at 6-12 months, and 13 ACLR scans at 12+ months were analyzed. Mean ages were 34.5, 34.5, and 37.2 years; female/male counts were 15/15, 9/10, and 8/5. FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: Participants underwent 3-T knee MRI with 3D fat-saturated UTE-Adiab-T1rho and UTE magnetization transfer sequences. ASSESSMENT: UTE-Adiab-T1rho and UTE-MMF maps were generated with single-component exponential and two-pool magnetization transfer models. Values were extracted from four meniscal regions of interest by a blinded reader, with blinded redelineation in a subset. Patient-reported outcomes included International Knee Documentation Committee, Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index scores. STATISTICAL TESTS: Linear mixed-effects models accounted for repeated observations. Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction was applied. RESULTS: UTE-Adiab-T1rho showed significant group (q = 0.001) and region (q < 0.001) effects. Compared with controls, UTE-Adiab-T1rho was higher in LAM at 6-12 months (+5.60 ms; q = 0.035) and 12+ months (+7.09 ms; q = 0.028), and in LPM at 12+ months (+6.35 ms; q = 0.035). UTE-MMF showed significant group (q = 0.041) and region (q < 0.001) effects. LPM UTE-MMF was lower than controls at 6-12 months (-3.56 percentage points; q = 0.028) and 12+ months (-3.10 percentage points; q = 0.049). No 6-12 versus 12+ month MRI or PROM contrast survived FDR correction. MRI-PROM associations were not FDR-significant (all q ≥ 0.383). DATA CONCLUSION: UTE-Adiab-T1rho and UTE-MMF mapping identified regional MRI differences after ACLR. Pairwise differences were concentrated in lateral regions, but corrected group-by-region interactions were not significant. PROMs were worse after ACLR but did not differ between postoperative windows after correction. EVIDENCE LEVEL: 2. TECHNICAL EFFICACY STAGE: 2.

metadata.title: The Potential Impact of Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors on Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness: A Prospective Cohort Study.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are widely prescribed for mood disorders. Their association with musculoskeletal side effects raises the question of potential SSRI impact on exercise-induced muscle damage and recovery. OBJECTIVE: The purpose of this prospective cohort study was to determine if SSRI use influences muscle function following a bout of eccentric exercise designed to induce delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS). METHODS: Subjects between 18 and 30 years of age were recruited in a university setting. This included 1 group taking SSRIs prescribed by their health care provider, and a control group not using SSRIs. Subjects performed a DOMS induction protocol consisting of 300 eccentric knee extensions on an isokinetic dynamometer. Muscle soreness, thigh circumference, quadriceps flexibility, and isometric quadriceps strength were measured at baseline and at 24-, 48-, 72-, and 96-hour post-DOMS protocol. Comparisons were made between SSRI users and control subjects. RESULTS: Thirty-six subjects included 18 SSRI users and 18 controls. The DOMS protocol induced muscle soreness in both groups (P < .001 when compared with baseline). At 72 hours a between-group difference was observed for thigh muscle flexibility (MD = 11.2, SE = 5.0, 95% CI [0.9, 21.4], P = .033, ηp2 = .126) but no additional significant between-group differences in soreness, strength, thigh circumference, or flexibility were noted at any timepoint. CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: In this population, SSRI use had no effect on muscle soreness, circumference, or strength of the quadriceps following eccentric DOMS-inducing exercise. A difference in flexibility between SSRI and control groups at a single time point likely reflects a Type 1 error and is not likely of clinical consequence. These findings suggest SSRIs do not impair short-term recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage in healthy young adults, but potential SSRI impacts on longer-term training adaptations and recovery in athletic populations remain unknown.

metadata.title: Conceptual Frameworks and Assessment of Readiness to Train in Endurance Exercise: A Systematic Review.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: Readiness to train has emerged as a construct to guide daily training prescription and recovery management in endurance athletes. However, its conceptual basis, assessment, and methodological quality and validity remain inconsistently defined. This systematic review aimed to (1) identify how readiness is defined in endurance exercise and (2) categorize tools used to assess it. As a secondary aim, the review evaluated the methodological approach of the studies employing these tools. METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were explored. Eligible studies included endurance athletes aged 18-65 years, evaluating readiness before or after training or competition. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed quality using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Fourteen studies were included. RESULTS: Readiness definitions were inconsistent and frequently overlapped with related constructs such as recovery and fatigue. Ten studies used self-reported tools (fatigue, sleep, stress, and soreness). Nine studies assessed objective tools, including heart rate (HR) variability, resting HR, countermovement jump, and submaximal tests. HR variability-based approaches and individualized feedback were used to track autonomic recovery and guide training prescription, while on-field indices (eg, HR-running speed, HR-running power, countermovement jump) provided neuromuscular insights, although they can also be influenced by cardiovascular and metabolic factors. Overall, there was considerable heterogeneity in tools and their combinations, highlighting the lack of standardized approaches to assess readiness to train. Seven studies combined subjective and objective measures, suggesting a more comprehensive monitoring strategy. However, many of these tools were primarily used to assess related constructs (eg, fatigue, recovery, and training adaptation) rather than directly predict performance; consequently, their ability to predict performance outcomes remained limited or was not even assessed. CONCLUSION: This review highlights substantial conceptual ambiguity, methodological limitations, and heterogeneity in readiness assessment. A multidimensional framework conceptualizing readiness as a dynamic psychophysiological state influenced by stress, recovery, and contextual factors may support more structured and meaningful monitoring in endurance athletes.

metadata.title: Discussing pain increases at the point of exercise prescription: a clinical commentary for persistent musculoskeletal conditions.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Patients with persistent musculoskeletal pain frequently perform prescribed exercise without direct supervision. When exercise increases symptoms, patients may be uncertain whether to continue, modify the session, or seek advice. A prescription that specifies exercises and dosage but provides no guidance about possible symptom aggravation may therefore leave an important gap in preparation. PURPOSE: This commentary proposes that, when prescribed exercise may increase pain, the possible response should be discussed at the point of prescription and that clinicians should prepare patients for how symptom aggravation will be interpreted and reviewed. DISCUSSION AND RECOMMENDATIONS: Trials comparing painful and nonpainful exercise, including an updated 2025 systematic review, show no consistent advantage for either approach and provide no basis for a universal adjustment rule. Pain-monitoring protocols developed for Achilles tendinopathy indicate that continued loading can be compatible with recovery in that condition, but their thresholds have not been validated for other presentations and should not be transferred by default. Features of altered nociceptive processing may further complicate interpretation of symptom aggravation but do not remove the need for assessment. What is proposed is a conversation rather than an algorithm: an explicit discussion, established when exercise is prescribed, about what a symptom increase might mean, how it will be interpreted, and when and how the plan will be reviewed. The evidence considered spans low back pain, osteoarthritis, and tendinopathy; extension to other persistent musculoskeletal conditions remains a reasonable but untested proposition. CONCLUSION: Research should establish what instructions clinicians currently provide when exercise increases pain, whether patients understand them, and which responses lead patients to continue, modify, or abandon exercise. Future studies should also determine whether discussing possible aggravation before it occurs improves adherence, confidence, function, and timely reassessment.

metadata.title: Noninvasive assessment of the anaerobic threshold in endurance athletes: an evidence-based narrative review of methods, validity, and field feasibility.
metadata.abstract: INTRODUCTION OR BACKGROUND: The anaerobic threshold (AnT) marks the transition between heavy and severe exercise intensity domains and guides training prescription and performance monitoring. Criterion methods (blood lactate and gas exchange) are accurate but invasive, costly, or impractical outside laboratories, prompting the search for noninvasive surrogates. This review evaluates the validity of these estimation procedures rather than the underlying physiology. SOURCES OF DATA: MEDLINE (via PubMed) was searched from inception without language restrictions, supplemented by reference-list and citation searching. Eligible studies compared noninvasive AnT indices, including heart rate variability (HRV; including detrended fluctuation analysis [DFA] α1), cardiac repolarization instability, heart rate deflection/field slope-variation methods, critical power (CP)/ critical speed (CS), near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), the talk test, and machine-learning (ML) models, with criterion standards. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Eighty-eight reports were synthesized narratively; no meta-analysis was performed. AREAS OF AGREEMENT: DFA α1, NIRS breakpoints, and CP/CS show strong associations with laboratory criteria and increasing field applicability through wearables. Accuracy and feasibility trade-offs require method selection according to the threshold, sport, and required precision. AREAS OF CONTROVERSY: Correlation indicates group-level association rather than individual agreement; Bland-Altman and reliability analyses are more informative for substitution. Criterion standards are not interchangeable, and heart rate deflection is not consistently identifiable. Evidence in female athletes remains limited. GROWING POINTS: Multimodal wearables integrating HRV, muscle oxygenation, and running power with ML may improve field-based threshold estimation. AREAS FOR DEVELOPING RESEARCH: Priorities include standardized reporting, transparent bias assessment, female-athlete validation, and broader systematic and meta-analytic synthesis.
