metadata.title: The content and reporting completeness of physical therapist-led interventions for glenohumeral osteoarthritis: a systematic review.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study synthesised the content and reporting completeness of published physical therapist-led interventions for glenohumeral osteoarthritis (GHOA). METHODS: This systematic review undertook electronic database searches in PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane, CINAHL and PEDro (until June 2025) for any peer-reviewed articles/studies describing physical therapist-led interventions across non-surgical and perioperative settings for adults aged 45 years and over with GHOA. The content and reporting completeness were synthesized using the 22-item Template for Intervention Description and Replication for rehabilitation interventions (TIDIeR_Rehab). RESULTS: Overall, 134 articles/studies describing 156 physical therapist-led interventions were included, comprising mostly case series designs (n=47, 35.1%) or narrative reviews (n=38, 28.4%). Of the remaining 49 articles/studies, only 11 were studies reporting RCT results and three were protocols of RCTs in progress. Intervention content varied considerably, and the overall completeness of intervention item reporting was poor (only 18%). Interventions in non-surgical contexts commonly included strengthening exercises (n=33, 53.2%), range of motion (ROM) exercises (n=23, 37.1%), and electrotherapy modalities (n=16, 25.8%). Sling immobilisation was most reported in postoperative interventions (n=64, 72.7%). Many different proposed mechanisms of action were reported (n=49, 31.4%); but all were biomechanically orientated. CONCLUSION: Very few high-quality empirical studies evaluating physical therapist-led interventions for GHOA have been published. We found substantial heterogeneity in the content of published physical therapist-led interventions, and the reporting completeness was generally poor. This suggests considerable uncertainty regarding best practice physical therapy for GHOA in terms of intervention content. Future high-quality empirical research is needed, preferably using RCT designs that include clear descriptions of interventions.

metadata.title: Reliability and validity of the My Jump Lab app for assessing vertical jump performance after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: To evaluate the test-retest reliability and validity of My Jump Lab compared with a force platform for assessing vertical jump performance after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). METHODS: A total of 102 individuals, 6-24 months post-ACLR and cleared for return-to-sport (RTS) testing, performed the single-leg vertical jump (SLVJ) and single-leg drop jump (SLDJ), assessed using My Jump Lab and a force platform. Jump height derived from flight time (FT) and take-off velocity (ToV), reactive strength index (RSI) and limb symmetry index (LSI) were analyzed. Test-retest reliability, inter-instrument reliability, agreement and association, diagnostic accuracy, and association with force-platform-derived kinetic (force at zero velocity, peak landing force, and concentric net impulse) variables were assessed. RESULTS: My Jump Lab demonstrated excellent test-retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) = 0.992-0.997; standard error of measurement = 0.24-0.41 cm; minimal detectable change = 0.65-1.14 cm). Associations with the force platform were strong to very strong for jump height (r = 0.786-0.987), RSI (r = 0.975), and LSI (r = 0.760-0.983). Inter-instrument reliability was excellent for FT and RSI (ICC = 0.974-0.983) and fair for ToV (ICC = 0.750). Bland-Altman analyses showed mean biases ranging from -1.21 to -0.08 cm for jump height and -0.29 cm/s for RSI. Accuracy for LSI ≥ 90% ranged from 87.3% to 94.1%. SLVJ jump height showed moderate-to-good associations with force-platform-derived kinetic (r = 0.534-0.678). CONCLUSIONS: My Jump Lab provides reliable and valid measures of vertical jump performance post-ACLR and may complement RTS assessment when force platforms are unavailable.

metadata.title: Surgical Profiles of Elite Female Athletes and Their Association with Long-Term Musculoskeletal Health: Findings from the Women's Soccer Health Study.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: To describe the career and post-career surgeries in female elite-level soccer players and evaluate their association with long-term musculoskeletal health. STUDY DESIGN: This is a cross-sectional study. METHODS: Surgical data (the number and type of surgeries during and after the career) from an anonymous online survey was obtained from a previously published cohort of 560 retired elite women's soccer players. Correlation coefficients were used to evaluate the relationship between the number of surgeries and physical activity levels (UCLA activity scale), joint function (SANE), and physical and mental health (PROMIS-10), which were all collected on the same survey. RESULTS: The average number of career surgeries was 1 (SD=1.6), and the average number of post-career surgeries was 0.5 (SD=1). The most common career surgery sites for women's soccer players were knee (39%), foot/ankle (12%), and leg (4%). The most common knee procedures involved ligament reconstruction, primarily of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), followed by meniscus and cartilage surgery. The most frequent post-career surgery sites were knee (24.0%), foot/ankle (5.1%), and leg (3.2%). Knee ligament and meniscus surgeries were equally reported. More career and post-career surgeries were associated with lower SANE knee scores (p<0.001). Lower SANE knee scores (p=0.017) were associated with lower UCLA activity levels. CONCLUSIONS: The locations of career and post-career surgeries were similar, suggesting a possible association with long-term musculoskeletal impairment, particularly to the knee, in a cohort of mostly White collegiate former players. Having more soccer-related surgeries was associated with reduced joint function and activity levels after retirement, though the correlations were weak or moderate. These findings suggest the need for the development of preventive interventions that address the specific needs of female athletes, implementation of injury prevention programs and strategies to maximize adherence, and long-term musculoskeletal assessments of players after retirement.

metadata.title: Age-Related Patterns of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Symptoms and Key Performance Factors in Adolescent Biathletes.
metadata.abstract: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) impairs health and performance, but age-related patterns in its emergence remain unclear. This study examines RED symptoms in adolescent biathletes at season-start and their link to end-of-season performance. A national cross-sectional study including prospective performance registration recruited biathletes to complete validated questionnaires, followed by clinical interviews if eating disorders (EDs) were indicated. Athletes ≥ 18 years were invited for physical laboratory assessments. End-of-season results were retrieved from open records. Analyses were performed by elastic net regression to identify the most stable predictors of performance, which were finally included in a linear regression model. Seventy-two athletes (55% females) with mean (SD) age 17.8 (1.4) years, 13.3 (3.3) training hours/week, and representing median (min, max) tier 3.0 (2, 5) were included. Prevalence in symptoms of low energy availability (LEA) was 18%, REDs 32%, EDs 11% (20% among females), and of depression 15%. Among 28 athletes (43% female) completing laboratory assessments, 11% had low BMD and ≤ 25% had clinical metabolic markers. Symptoms of mental health issues and REDs were more common in females and the older age groups. Higher training volume and low RED severity positively predicted performance, whereas injury/illness-related training absences, cholesterol, and body fat percentage negatively affected race results. RED symptoms are common in young biathletes. Illness/injury-related training absences were frequent and linked to poorer end-of-season performance, underscoring the need for routine screening by health- and performance teams to detect and manage early symptoms of LEA, reduce RED risk, and prevent premature career termination.

metadata.title: Surgery under fire: war injuries and the consequences of delayed care in Ethiopia's Tigray region.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: The armed conflict in Ethiopia, particularly in the Tigray region, has caused a substantial burden of war-related injuries in the context of a fragile and disrupted health system. Restricted access to timely surgical care has resulted in delayed presentation and may contribute to secondary complications, contractures, peripheral nerve dysfunction, and long-term disability. However, the consequences of delayed surgical treatment for conflict-related extremity trauma in active war settings remain insufficiently described. This study aimed to characterize conflict-related injuries in Mek'ele, Ethiopia, with a particular focus on delayed surgical care, peripheral nerve injuries, and reconstructive needs. METHODS: This retrospective observational study was conducted between September and December 2023 at Ayder Comprehensive Specialized Hospital in Mek'ele, the capital city of Ethiopia's Tigray region. Patients presenting with conflict-related injuries were identified through routine clinical documentation. Epidemiological characteristics, prior surgical interventions, presenting complaints, clinical findings, and diagnoses were recorded. Peripheral nerve injuries and reconstructive challenges were analyzed in detail. Surgical treatment plans were categorized into reconstructive, corrective and functional, tendon and muscle, nerve, scar and contracture, limb or tissue removal, and supportive procedures. Group comparisons were performed using chi-square and Fisher's exact tests, and logistic regression models were used to estimate relative likelihoods. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. RESULTS: A total of 197 conflict-related injuries were analyzed, including 108 bullet injuries (54.8%) and 82 blast injuries (41.6%). Peripheral nerve injuries were identified in 54.3% of patients. Bullet injuries were more strongly associated with movement restriction, functional deficits, and peripheral nerve damage, whereas blast injuries were more frequently linked to fractures, soft tissue defects, pain, and scars or wounds. Blast injuries more often required reconstructive procedures and contracture release, while bullet injuries more frequently required corrective and functional surgery. Because most patients presented months to years after injury, primary nerve repair was rarely feasible, resulting in a high demand for secondary salvage procedures such as tendon transfers and muscle transpositions. CONCLUSIONS: Conflict-related extremity trauma in Tigray is characterized not only by injury mechanism but also by the consequences of delayed access to surgical care. Missed opportunities for early definitive treatment contributed to a high burden of peripheral nerve deficits, contractures, reconstructive needs, and long-term functional impairment. Improving access to acute trauma care, early nerve repair, reconstructive surgery, and rehabilitation is essential to reduce disability in conflict-affected settings.

metadata.title: Objective Return-to-Sport (RTS) Decision Frameworks for Adolescent Shoulder and Elbow Injuries: Tests, Thresholds and Exercise Targets.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Adolescent shoulder and elbow injuries are increasing due to sports specialization and year-round training, yet return-to-sport decisions typically rely on adult-derived heuristics that fail to address the unique physiology, growth plate vulnerability, and recovery needs of developing athletes aged 10-19 years. OBJECTIVE: This review proposes a novel, objective three-pillar RTS framework integrating: (1) foundational tissue capacity, (2) dynamic movement quality and neuromuscular control, and (3) sport-specific load tolerance. We synthesize current evidence to establish provisional, consensus-based adolescent thresholds and provide a practical bedside toolkit for immediate clinical implementation. METHODS: We conducted a narrative synthesis of contemporary original evidence, consensus recommendations, and validation studies relevant to adolescent shoulder and elbow rehabilitation. Evidence was critically appraised for youth-specific validation, with explicit distinction between evidence-based interventions and emerging aspirational technologies requiring prospective adolescent cohort validation. RESULTS: We propose a hybrid benchmarking model combining limb symmetry indices (LSI ≥90%) with population-referenced percentiles (≥25th percentile for age/sex/sport) as provisional, consensus-based thresholds. A three-stage progression is outlined: Clinic-ready (pain-free ROM, isometric IR/ER LSI ≥90%), Training-ready (dynamic rotational LSI ≥90%, preserved scapular kinematics), and Game-ready (sport-specific tolerance with 5% velocity loss during simulated exposure). We provide a low-resource bedside toolkit including belt-stabilized hand-held dynamometry, Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test (CKCUEST), Push-Up Plus, Athletic Shoulder positions, seated medicine-ball throw, and simple interval tolerance simulations with specific protocols and thresholds. A stepwise algorithm advances from capacity → movement quality → load tolerance with targeted remediation at each gate. CONCLUSION: Moving beyond time-based or adult-derived heuristics, this objective multidimensional framework aligns tissue recovery with sport-specific demands through quantifiable metrics. While provisional thresholds require further adolescent validation, the framework offers an evidence-guided pathway that mitigates reinjury risk, restores performance, and supports safe reintegration into sport. Implementation requires adolescent-specific normative databases, stakeholder communication, and cost-effective technological integration for equitable adoption.

metadata.title: Muscle biomechanical rehabilitation following therapy in Achilles and patellar tendinopathy assessed by MR elastography.
metadata.abstract: Tendon healing is the primary goal of tendinopathy therapy. However, the therapeutic response of adjacent muscles remains uninvestigated. MR-elastography (MRE) can assess muscle biomechanical properties and function. This study investigated muscle biomechanical responses in patients treated for patellar (PT) or Achilles tendinopathy (AT). A prospective longitudinal study included 20 athletes, 8 with AT (41 years ± 8; 6 men) and 12 with PT (34 years ± 10; 12 men), who underwent MRI, diffusion-tensor-imaging (DTI), and MRE before and ≥6 months post-treatment. Isotropic (ciso) and anisotropic stiffness parameters (c‖ and c⊥) in tendon-adjacent muscles were derived and analyzed between groups and longitudinally compared with clinical scores and tendon dimensions. At baseline, symptomatic legs with higher tendon dimensions and clinical symptoms exhibited lower muscle stiffness than asymptomatic legs (p<0.05). Post-treatment, AT patients showed increased ciso (4.3±8.5%) in gastrocnemius and posterior soleus (SolP; 4.9±8.6%) in treated legs but decreased SolP stiffness (-3.2±7.2%) in untreated legs (p<0.05). In PT patients, only anisotropic MRE (c‖: 5.3±15.2% and c⊥: 10.3±12.7%) in vastus lateralis showed significant increases (p<0.05) post-treatment. In treated legs of AT and PT, increased muscle stiffness post-treatment correlated negatively with tendon dimensions (p<0.05). Post-therapy, tendon-adjacent muscles exhibited increased stiffness in affected leg and decreased stiffness in contralateral leg (particularly SolP), potentially reflecting altered muscle use and loading, respectively. The observed changes in muscle stiffness may help characterize muscle biomechanical changes during rehabilitation and balanced recovery. Furthermore, anisotropic muscle stiffness was more sensitive to tendon structural changes than isotropic stiffness, warranting further validation for clinical assessment.

metadata.title: Short-term effects of extracorporeal shockwave therapy and low-level laser therapy on clinical outcomes and ultrasonographic tendon thickness in lateral elbow tendinopathy.
metadata.abstract: BackgroundThis study aimed to compare the short-term effects of extracorporeal shock wave therapy (ESWT) and low-level laser therapy (LLLT) on pain, elbow function, health-related quality of life, hand grip strength, and ultrasonographic extensor tendon thickness in patients with LET.ObjectiveIn this prospective, randomized, controlled, single-blind trial, patients with LET were randomly assigned to either ESWT or LLLT. Both groups received the same standardized home exercise program and lateral epicondylitis brace. Visual Analog Scale (VAS), the Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation (PRTEE), Short Form-36 (SF-36), hand grip strength, and ultrasonographic evaluation were assessed before and after three weeks of randomisation.ResultsAt three weeks, the ESWT group demonstrated significantly lower post-treatment pain intensity (VAS) than the LLLT group (p = 0.004). ESWT was also associated with significantly better outcomes in PRTEE pain scores (p = 0.030), ultrasonographic tendon thickness (p = 0.021), and the Role Physical (p = 0.029) and General Health (p = 0.005) domains of the SF-36. No significant between-group differences were observed in hand grip strength, PRTEE function, PRTEE total score, or the remaining SF-36 domains.ConclusionWhen used as adjuncts to a standardized exercise program and LET brace, ESWT was associated with greater short-term pain reduction and more favorable outcomes in the PRTEE pain subscale, ultrasonographic tendon thickness, and selected domains of health-related quality of life compared with LLLT. These findings suggest that ESWT may offer greater short-term pain-related benefits than LLLT when both are added to exercise and bracing.

metadata.title: Orthobiologics in Focus: Current Evidence, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions, A Scoping Review.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Regenerative modalities are increasingly becoming part of orthopedic practice with the use of orthobiologic interventions. These interventions make use of biological approaches to help in repairing the tissues, mitigating nociception, and improving locomotor performance. OBJECTIVE: The current scoping review is a review of the modern literature as of 2020-2025 on orthobiologic therapies. It examines their clinical effectiveness, the strength of supporting evidence, and the development of new progress in musculoskeletal pathology regenerative management. METHODS: A systematic search in PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and WoS was done on the articles with their indexes dated between January 2020 and February 2025. The inclusion criteria were human and animal studies that utilized platelet-rich plasma (PRP), (MSCs), bone marrow aspirate concentrate (BMAC), and adipose-derived products strategies using a scaffold only. Synthesis and data extraction were conducted as per PRISMA-ScR standards. RESULTS: Among the 1716 records that had been filtered, 81 studies met inclusion criteria. Most of them were randomized or comparative trials (77% Level I-II evidence), which are evidence of the high methodological quality. PRP was the most commonly researched modality, whereas MSC-based interventions were the most common. CONCLUSION: PRP, MSCs, and BMAC are orthobiologic modalities, which are evidence-based and effective alternatives to promote musculoskeletal healing and regeneration. These interventions supplemented by conventional surgical procedures and rehabilitative interventions yield pain relief, functional restoration, and long-term joint maintenance in a spectrum of orthopedic complications.

metadata.title: Uefa consensus guidelines on anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in women's football - Part Two: rehabilitation, return to play, and players' perceptions.
metadata.abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries remain a major challenge to player health and performance in women's football. They are associated with lengthy rehabilitation, a high risk of re-injury, and potential long-term knee issues that can impact both career longevity and quality of life. Building on Part One of the UEFA consensus, which addressed risk factors and prevention, Part Two addresses the continuum of care after ACL injury, from rehabilitation to return to play (RTP) and beyond. A multidisciplinary panel of 26 experts in sports medicine, physiotherapy, orthopaedics, and performance science developed evidence-informed statements using a modified RAND-UCLA Appropriateness Method. Through three Delphi rounds, 180 statements were assessed and refined, resulting in consensus on 170 (94%). The panel supported a player-centred, criterion-based approach where progression relies on clinical and functional milestones rather than fixed timelines. Key recommendations emphasise restoring quadriceps strength as a central milestone, integrating neuromuscular and psychological readiness assessments, and adopting phased RTP protocols that gradually re-expose players to the physical and cognitive demands of the game. Psychological and social factors (fear of re-injury, motivation, communication, and support networks) are recognised as vital influences on recovery. These guidelines offer practical, evidence-based advice for medical and performance staff working in women's football. By combining scientific research with expert consensus, they support a holistic, collaborative approach to ACL rehabilitation aimed at protecting player health, lowering re-injury risk, and enabling a confident, sustained return to performance.

metadata.title: Isometric Strength, Joint Mobility, and Muscle Strength Ratios Among Female Artistic Swimmers from the Spanish National Artistic Swimming Team: A Cross-Sectional Study Across Age Categories.
metadata.abstract: Background and Objectives: Artistic swimming demands high levels of strength, joint mobility, and body control; however, the physical profiles of elite athletes in this sport remain insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to characterize and compare isometric strength, joint mobility, inter-limb differences, and muscle strength ratios across the Youth, Junior, and Senior age categories of the Spanish National Artistic Swimming Team. Methods: This cross-sectional observational study included 36 elite female artistic swimmers, defined by their selection for the Spanish National Artistic Swimming Team: 11 Youth, 12 Junior, and 13 Senior athletes. Anthropometric characteristics, shoulder and hip ranges of motion assessed using photographic goniometry, upper- and lower-limb isometric strength, handgrip strength, and countermovement jump height were evaluated. Age categories were compared using the Kruskal-Wallis test, followed by Dunn's post hoc comparisons with Holm correction. Inter-limb differences were analyzed using the Wilcoxon test. Results: Senior athletes generally exhibited greater isometric strength than younger age categories. Among the main between-category differences, Senior athletes showed greater normalized shoulder internal-rotation strength than Youth athletes (1.56 vs. 0.95 N/kg; group-specific 95% CIs around the means: 1.43-1.69 and 0.80-1.11, respectively) and greater hip-abduction strength (2.34 vs. 1.71 N/kg; group-specific 95% CIs around the means: 2.07-2.60 and 1.51-1.93, respectively). The corresponding omnibus Kruskal-Wallis effect sizes were η2 = 0.40 and η2 = 0.32, respectively. Differences were observed in CMJ height and absolute right handgrip strength. No significant differences were observed after normalizing handgrip strength to body mass. Between-category differences were observed in certain measures of hip mobility but not in shoulder mobility. Inter-limb differences were limited to specific variables. Conclusions: These findings provide a preliminary descriptive characterization of elite female artistic swimmers and reveal differences between age categories, primarily in specific strength variables. These cross-sectional differences between age categories should not be interpreted as evidence of developmental adaptations or training-induced changes. Given the cross-sectional design and small group sizes, the application of these findings to athlete monitoring, training, or the interpretation of inter-limb differences requires confirmation in longitudinal studies.

metadata.title: Autologous Peripheral Blood-Derived Stem Cells Combined with Platelet-Rich Plasma is Associated With Clinical and Radiological Improvement in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Ruptures-Preliminary Clinical and MRI Findings in 47 Consecutive Patients.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) ruptures are common injuries in young and active individuals and can lead to long-term functional impairment and early onset osteoarthritis. While ACL reconstruction remains the standard of care, recent evidence suggests that spontaneous healing may be possible in selected cases. Regenerative and biologic treatment concepts have therefore gained increasing interest. This study investigates the clinical and radiological outcomes of a stem cell-based regenerative treatment for traumatic ACL ruptures and presents findings as preliminary observational evidence. METHODS: In this single-center retrospective case series, 47 patients with isolated partial and complete traumatic anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) ruptures were treated using a biologic, non-surgical protocol. Diagnosis of an ACL rupture was confirmed by standardized clinical examination (Lachman test, anterior drawer test, and pivot shift test) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which was additionally used to assess rupture morphology and synovial sheath integrity. All patients underwent an ultrasound-guided injection of autologous biologic products derived from peripheral venous blood, consisting of 8 mL of an autologous blood-derived stem cell preparation (BSC), comprising approximately 2-3 mL of concentrated mononuclear cells suspended in 6 mL of autologous platelet-containing plasma, injected directly into the torn ACL. Patients were allowed immediate full weight-bearing without bracing and followed a standardized physiotherapy program. Clinical follow-up was conducted for 12 months, including assessment of pain (VAS), functional outcomes (IKDC, Lysholm), return-to-sport timelines, and MRI-based evaluation of ligament morphology. RESULTS: The mean age of the cohort was 28.1 years (95% CI 26.0-30.2). Functional outcomes improved continuously throughout follow-up, with mean IKDC and Lysholm scores of 93.6 (95% CI 92.4-94.8) and 94.0 (95% CI 92.7-95.3), respectively, at 12 months. Pain levels decreased markedly, reaching a mean VAS score of 0.36 (95% CI 0.19-0.53). Patients returned to running after a mean of 2.19 weeks (95% CI 1.93-2.45), and most resumed their pre-injury activity level by one year. No infections or re-ruptures occurred and only one secondary ACL reconstruction was recorded. Patients with an intact synovial sheath demonstrated faster return to pivoting sports (26.8 vs. 33.2 weeks) compared with patients with a complete ACL rupture. MRI at 3 months showed evidence of improved ligament morphology in all but one patient. CONCLUSIONS: This preliminary case series suggests that stem cell-based biologic stimulation may be associated with functional recovery and radiological improvement in selected patients with ACL ruptures. Prospective controlled trials are required to validate these findings.

metadata.title: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy State of pathology: Insertional tendon tendinopathies.
metadata.abstract: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy (IAT) is a common but disabling pathology affecting both athletes and older subjects. The aim of the present study was to provide a practical review of IA, addressing the following questions: What are the etiologies and pathophysiology? Etiology is multifactorial, involving anatomic aspects and especially posterosuperior calcaneal prominence, biomechanical aspects such as short triceps surae, pes cavus or hindfoot varus, extrinsic aspects of footwear and overtraining, and metabolic aspects. Pathophysiology, depending on the individual case, implicates true insertional tendinopathy and posterior bone-tendon impingement to varying degrees, often with pre-Achilles bursitis; the distinction is crucial to decision-making. Impingement or enthesopathy lead to progressive disorganization of the collagen matrix, pathologic neovascularization and mucoid degeneration of the tendon, often with intratendon calcifications and inflammatory retrocalcaneal bursitis. How to establish diagnosis? Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on pain location, which is median in case of insertional tendinopathy and more lateral in case of posterior impingement with bursitis. Examination finds pain on palpation of the Achilles insertion, sometimes with local thickening, posterior tumefaction and painful restriction of ankle dorsiflexion. Tensing the tendon typically reproduces the pain. Functional tests may show restriction due to pain, without tendon tear. Weight-bearing X-ray, ultrasound and especially MRI analyze the respective roles of bone, tendon and bursa injury; weight-bearing CT can be contributive in some morphologically complex situations. Ultrasound reveals tendon thickening, hypoechogenic degenerative areas, hypervascularization on Doppler and associated bursitis. MRI shows lesion extension: intratendon degeneration, deep fiber involvement and retrocalcaneal inflammation. What are the non-operative treatments? Initial treatment is conservative, based on adapting weight-bearing and footwear, with exercises adapted to the form of the insertion, extracorporeal shock waves and rehabilitation. What are the surgical options and their expected results? In case of failure of well-conducted non-operative treatment, surgical strategy depends on lesion type, degree of posterior impingement, degree of tendon degeneration and degree of triceps surae stiffness. Expected results comprise pain relief, functional improvement on VISA-A score, and progressive return to activities, with timing depending on the technique and the initial level of activity. How to choose the surgical treatment? Surgical options comprise bone decompression, debridement and tendon reinsertion, flexor hallucis longus transfer and gastrocnemius lengthening depending on lesion type on clinical examination and imaging.

metadata.title: Platelet-related extracellular vesicles: Therapeutic roles in musculoskeletal disorders.
metadata.abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders are a major cause of pain, disability, and loss of function. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been widely investigated for musculoskeletal repair, and interest has increasingly extended to extracellular vesicle (EV) preparations obtained from platelet-related starting materials. These include EV-enriched preparations collected from isolated platelets or defined platelet concentrates (P-EVs), from PRP (PRP-EVs), and from platelet lysate (PL-EVs). They do not represent the same biological product. Their cellular contributors, co-isolated soluble components, and molecular composition can differ substantially, and the name of the starting material does not prove the origin of every vesicle in the preparation. Preclinical studies nevertheless suggest that these EV preparations can influence inflammatory responses, cartilage metabolism, tendon-cell behavior, and the local repair environment. The strength of this evidence varies with the source material, separation and characterization methods, experimental model, and delivery strategy. This review examines the therapeutic evidence for platelet-related EV preparations in musculoskeletal disorders, while keeping P-EVs, PRP-EVs, PL-EVs, and plasma-derived EVs distinct and considering the methodological limitations that currently restrict comparison and clinical translation.

metadata.title: A Narrative Review of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Graft Choice and Its Influence on Return to Sport.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture is among the most common knee injuries in active individuals and can lead to persistent instability, secondary intra-articular damage, and an elevated risk of osteoarthritis. Because return to sport (RTS) is a major goal for most active patients and graft selection remains one of the most debated aspects of ACL reconstruction, this narrative review summarizes the contemporary evidence on how graft choice influences RTS, focusing on the four most common grafts: bone-patellar tendon-bone (BTB), hamstring tendon (HT), quadriceps tendon (QT), and allograft. RECENT FINDINGS: RTS rates range from ~ 65% to 73% at three years and are higher (83-90%) in elite and high-school athletes. In young, active patients, autografts are associated with higher RTS and lower revision rates than allografts, and high-level evidence-including randomized-trial meta-analyses-has not established the superiority of any single autograft. BTB offers reliable bone-to-bone healing and low revision rates; HT reduces donor-site morbidity and anterior knee pain but has variable diameter and possible flexion weakness; and QT is a versatile option with favorable biomechanics, low donor-site morbidity, and encouraging RTS data, including in skeletally immature athletes. RTS is one of several important outcomes after ACL reconstruction, alongside long-term joint health and reinjury prevention. For RTS, the literature supports autograft over allograft in young, active patients while identifying no universally superior autograft. Graft selection should be individualized to patient age, sport, activity level, anatomy, and reinjury risk; the senior author favors QT or BTB autografts for high-demand athletes.

metadata.title: Calf Injuries: Anatomy, Pathology, and Treatment.
metadata.abstract: Calf injuries are common in athletes and typically result in missed time from sport and activities of daily living. The three individual triceps surae muscles can be injured, with differing described mechanisms. Gastrocnemius or plantaris strains tend to occur during sudden explosive movement of the ankle from a dorsiflexed to a plantarflexed position with the knee in extension. Soleus strains typically occur from repetitive dorsiflexion of the ankle with the knee flexed. Imaging modalities such as magnetic resonance imaging and ultrasonography can be helpful in determining the location and grade of injury, which can aid in treatment and return to play timelines. Classically, these injuries have been graded as grade I, II, or III, with grade I having <10% muscle fiber disruption, grade II having >10 to 50% muscle fiber disruption, and grade III having 50 to 100% muscle fiber disruption. The mainstay of treatment for most calf strains is nonsurgical, with surgical management being rare but reported in the literature for isolated grade III ruptures of the medial head of the gastrocnemius. Return to sport and activities requires a graduated physical therapy program focused on restoring tissue length without excessive strain. Recent limited evidence has shown promising results with quicker return to activities and decreased pain with platelet-rich plasma injections.

metadata.title: Functional recovery of athletes through rehabilitation training after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: This article aims to introduce neuromuscular electrical stimulation into rehabilitation training after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and to assess its impact on the functional recovery of the knee joint. METHODS: Twenty athletes undergoing anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction were allocated into a neuromuscular electrical stimulation group (neuromuscular electrical stimulation + rehabilitation training) and a conventional group (conventional rehabilitation training) for a 10-week training program. Indicators such as Lysholm scores and thigh circumference were assessed before and after training for comparison. RESULTS: After training, the neuromuscular electrical stimulation group demonstrated a Lysholm score of 86.56 ± 11.67 points, a thigh circumference on the affected side of 47.15 ± 2.56 cm, and an active knee flexion angle of 105.12 ± 9.87°. Moreover, the score of the Y-balance test under left- and right-foot support was 93.67 ± 0.43 and 91.72 ± 0.48 points, respectively. It achieved a 10-meter walk speed of 1.01 ± 0.15 m/s. It achieved a performance of 264.39 ± 29.36 cm in three consecutive single-leg jumps on the healthy side and a performance of 178.16 ± 21.26 cm on the affected side. Its anterior cruciate ligament return-to-sport after injury scale score was 84.21 ± 5.32 points. These outcomes were significantly superior to those of the conventional group. CONCLUSIONS: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation combined with rehabilitation training yields positive effects on functional recovery after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, surpassing the outcomes of conventional rehabilitation training. This approach holds promise for practical application.

metadata.title: The Current State of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: Graft Selection, Lateral Augmentation, Rehabilitation, and Return-to-Play.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) reliably restores anteroposterior stability; however, the rate of return to prior level of play and incidence of recurrent ACL injury have improved little over the past two decades. The purpose of this review is to describe the current state of ACLR with respect to graft selection, lateral extra-articular augmentation, rehabilitation and return to play, including the role of psychological readiness, and the specific rehabilitation protocol utilized by the senior author. RECENT FINDINGS: Graft utilization has shifted substantially. Quadriceps tendon autograft accounted for less than 5% of primary reconstructions prior to 2014 and approximately 20% by 2023. Contemporary registry data demonstrate smaller differences in revision risk between autograft types than previously reported. Randomized and comparative data support lateral extra-articular tenodesis in selected high-risk knees, with the largest effect reported in the revision setting. Return-to-play practice has shifted from fixed timelines toward criteria-based clearance. However, a subset of athletes do not pass a full clearance battery, and some athletes who do pass and observe recommended timeframes still sustain reinjury. Limb symmetry index may overestimate functional recovery, while test batteries and thresholds vary considerably between institutions. Psychological readiness is independently associated with both return to sport and second ACL injury. Graft selection should be matched to the patient profile, and lateral augmentation should be reserved for high-risk knees. Return to play should be determined by a combination of time from surgery, functional criteria, and psychological readiness. Future study should focus on validating return-to-play criteria against reinjury endpoints and on standardizing how these criteria are defined and reported.

metadata.title: Attention allocation in team sports: A systematic review and meta-analysis based on eye-tracking.
metadata.abstract: Expert athletes are generally considered to exhibit distinct visual search behaviors and superior behavioral performance. However, findings regarding perceptual-cognitive differences across skill levels in team sports remain inconsistent. Therefore, this study aimed to systematically examine differences in visual search behavior and behavioral performance across skill levels in team sports. A systematic search was conducted in EBSCO, PubMed, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science, resulting in 26 eligible studies involving expert, intermediate, and novice athletes from football, basketball, and volleyball. A random-effects meta-analysis was performed using Hedges' g to estimate pooled effect sizes, and subgroup analyses were conducted to examine potential moderating factors. Results revealed that, for eye movement outcomes, only limited evidence supported a significant pooled effect for fixation duration across skill levels. Subgroup analyses based on a limited number of studies identified significant differences between intermediate and novice athletes, particularly in the number of fixations in basketball and volleyball. For behavioral performance, significant differences were observed in reaction time for expert-intermediate and expert-novice comparisons, whereas the overall effect for performance accuracy was not significant after publication bias adjustment. These findings suggest a complex relationship between visual characteristics and behavioral performance at different skill levels in team sports.

metadata.title: Creatine supplementation in soccer players: a systematic review.
metadata.abstract: AIM: Soccer places repeated demands on short-duration, high-intensity performance, including sprints, accelerations, jumps, and technical actions performed over the course of a match. Because these efforts depend heavily on rapid adenosine triphosphate (ATP) resynthesis, creatine is a plausible ergogenic aid for soccer players. However, findings in soccer-specific studies have been inconsistent, and previous reviews have addressed narrower questions using smaller evidence sets. This systematic review therefore examined the effects of creatine supplementation on performance, body composition, and recovery/fatigue-related outcomes in soccer players. METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to 15 May 2025 in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. We included controlled clinical trials of creatine supplementation in male or female soccer players of any age or competitive level when an eligible placebo, control, or comparison condition was available. Outcomes were grouped into performance, body composition, and recovery/fatigue domains. Domains from the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials (RoB 2) and the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomised Studies - of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool were used to produce study-level methodological summaries rather than formal result-specific risk-of-bias assessments. Because the studies differed substantially in design, supplementation protocols, populations, and outcomes, findings were synthesised qualitatively rather than pooled in a meta-analysis. RESULTS: Source-level verification left 45 eligible reports representing 41 unique studies: 28 randomised parallel-group studies, 2 randomised crossover/repeated-condition studies, and 11 non-randomised or allocation-unverifiable controlled studies. Some trials reported favourable findings for repeated-sprint performance, anaerobic power, and muscular strength, but the comparative evidence was inconsistent and the certainty of evidence was very low. Findings for vertical jump performance and technical skills were mixed, while change-of-direction and endurance outcomes showed no consistent benefit. Recovery- and fatigue-related findings were also largely null or inconsistent. Body mass often increased, particularly after loading protocols, whereas evidence for gains in lean mass was limited and inconsistent. CONCLUSION: The soccer-specific evidence for creatine supplementation remains suggestive rather than conclusive. Favourable findings have been reported for some repeated-sprint, anaerobic-power, and strength outcomes, but the comparative evidence is heterogeneous, often limited by unclear or nonsignificant between-group effects, and of very low certainty. Firm conclusions about efficacy are therefore not possible. Body mass commonly increased, especially after loading protocols, while effects on lean mass, endurance, change-of-direction ability, and recovery/fatigue-related outcomes remain uncertain.

metadata.title: [Translated article] Comparative analysis between intramedullary screw fixation and plate osteosynthesis in midshaft clavicle fractures: surgical efficiency and functional outcomes in contact athletes.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Plate fixation is the current gold standard for displaced midshaft clavicle fractures, despite concerns regarding surgical morbidity and implant prominence. The purpose of this study was to compare the clinical, radiographic, and surgical outcomes of an intramedullary screw system versus conventional plate fixation. METHODS: A comparative cohort study was performed on 72 patients (36 treated with the Screw system and 36 with plate fixation). Surgical variables (time and blood loss), radiographic consolidation (at 4, 8, and 12 weeks), and functional outcomes (DASH and Constant-Murley scores) were analyzed. Statistical significance was set at p < .05. RESULTS: The Screw group demonstrated a significantly shorter operative time (27.69+/- 9.39 vs. 105.47 +/- 55.18 minutes; p<.001) and minimal blood loss (10 vs. 228.33 ml; p<.001). Functional recovery was significantly faster in the DualTrack group, with an earlier return to physical activity (6.64 vs. 21.69 weeks; p<.001) and superior Constant scores (98.64 vs. 94.81; p = .0006). Radiographically, the screw group showed significantly lower fracture line visibility at 8 and 12 weeks compared to the plate group (p<.05). Complication rates were lower for the screw group (8.3%) than for the plate group (25.0%), although this did not reach statistical significance (p=.11). CONCLUSION: The intramedullary system is a highly effective alternative for clavicle fractures, providing superior surgical efficiency, faster functional recovery, and improved biological healing compared to conventional plate fixation. It should be considered a primary treatment option, particularly for patients seeking a rapid return to activity and minimally invasive surgery.

metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sprint interval training (SIT) effectively improves physical performance in team-sport athletes, while sodium bicarbonate (Sb) supplementation may enhance training adaptations. However, the dose-dependent effects of Sb during SIT remain unclear in basketball players. Therefore, this study examined the effects of two Sb doses combined with SIT on physical performance adaptations in basketball players. METHODS: Forty trained male basketball players (age: 21.6 ± 2.0 years, height: 185.4 ± 3.5 cm, body mass: 84.1 ± 4.4 kg) were recruited and randomly assigned to four groups: SIT + 0.3 g·kg-1 Sb (n = 10), SIT + 0.45 g·kg-1 Sb (n = 10), SIT + placebo (PL) (n = 10), and control (CON) (n = 10). The intervention lasted four weeks during the preparatory phase of the season. Participants in the training groups performed SIT three times per week in addition to their regular basketball training. The SIT protocol consisted of four sets of ten 5-second maximal sprints, with 20 seconds of active recovery between repetitions and 2 minutes of rest between sets. All 40 enrolled participants successfully completed the 4-week intervention, resulting in a 0% dropout rate. Performance assessments conducted before and after the intervention included countermovement vertical jump (CMVJ), standing long jump (SLJ), 20 m sprint, Illinois change-of-direction speed (CODS), Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 1 (Yo-Yo IR1), and Wingate anaerobic power (peak power output [PPO] and mean power output [MPO]). RESULTS: All training groups showed significant improvements in physical performance variables over time (p < 0.05). Significant group by time interaction effects were observed for all performance variables (p ≤ 0.001), indicating that the SIT groups showed more gains compared with the CON group. Both Sb supplementation groups demonstrated greater improvements than the SIT + PL group in CMVJ, SLJ, sprint performance, CODS, Yo-Yo IR1 distance, PPO, and MPO (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the SIT + 0.45 g·kg-1 Sb group exhibited significantly greater performance enhancements than the SIT + 0.3 g·kg-1 Sb group across all measured variables. CONCLUSION: Four weeks of SIT improved performance in trained basketball players, with Sb supplementation providing additional dose-dependent benefits (0.45 > 0.3 g⋅kg-1). While the higher dose yielded superior adaptations, its practical application should be balanced against potential gastrointestinal discomfort and individual tolerance to ensure long-term athlete compliance.

metadata.title: Changes in Hormone Cycles and Exercise Capacity During Testosterone Therapy in a Transmasculine Triathlete: A Case Study.
metadata.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The impact of testosterone therapy on the hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiology of transmasculine individuals is not well understood. Existing studies report limited metrics at large time intervals between data collection points. METHODS: High-resolution temporal data were collected from a single amateur trans male triathlete over 13 months-including one baseline month and 12 months on testosterone therapy-to characterize hormone, strength, body composition, aerobic, and training load profiles. RESULTS: Daily urine hormone monitoring revealed that progesterone and luteinizing hormone are the clearest metrics associated with cessation of menses. After 1 yr, the participant increased lean body mass by 12%, average hand grip strength by 16%, jump height by 16%, and average knee isometric strength by 18%, but did not lose fat mass or show changes in isokinetic knee strength. Fluctuations in running fitness and maximum oxygen consumption ( V ˙ O 2 m a x ) were associated with both training and testosterone levels, with future work needed to untangle their relative contributions. CONCLUSION: This study provides the most comprehensive characterization of the impacts of testosterone therapy on hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiological changes in a single person to date, as well as observations to help inform the design of larger cohort studies.

metadata.title: Low Physical Therapy Referral Rates for Knee Osteoarthritis Present a Barrier to Care for Patients With Medicaid.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the rates of physical therapy (PT) referral for knee osteoarthritis (KOA) and factors associated with referral patterns, including insurance status, provider specialty, year, and patient demographics and comorbidities. DESIGN: This retrospective cohort study included 41,373 patients diagnosed with KOA at an integrated health system in Arizona and Colorado, USA between January 2020 and February 2023. PT referral rates were stratified by insurance type. Multivariable logistic regression assessed predictors of referral including insurance type, age, BMI, sex, race/ethnicity, provider specialty, year of visit, and comorbidities. RESULTS: Crude PT referral rates at the initial visit were 12.06% for Medicaid, 6.83% for Medicare, 10.29% for commercial insurance, and 8.33% for uninsured patients. Adjusted analysis showed that Medicaid patients had higher referral odds (OR, 1.20; 95% CI [1.10, 1.30]; p < 0.001), whereas Medicare patients had lower odds (OR, 0.76; 95% CI [0.66, 0.88]; p < 0.001) compared to those with commercial insurance. Female (OR, 1.21; 95% CI [1.14, 1.29]; p < 0.001) and Hispanic patients (OR 1.18; 95% CI [1.09, 1.29]; p < 0.001) demonstrated increased referral odds. Provider specialty was associated with PT referral, with non-operative sports medicine providers having the highest referral odds (OR, 3.00; 95% CI [2.72, 3.31]; p < 0.001) relative to orthopaedic surgery. CONCLUSION: Despite strong clinical practice guidelines recommending PT, formal referral rates for patients with KOA remain low regardless of insurance type, patient characteristics, and referring healthcare provider specialty. Low formal PT referral rates may represent a barrier to evidence-based KOA care.

metadata.title: The Use of Cupping (Hijama) Therapy Among Athletes and Its Relationship With Sleep Quality: A Cross-Sectional Study in Palestine.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Wet cupping, or Hijama, is commonly used by athletes for recovery, yet evidence regarding its relationship with sleep quality remains limited. This study examined cupping use, perceived benefits, adverse effects, and factors associated with self-reported sleep quality among Palestinian athletes. METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among Palestinian athletes. Of 754 athletes screened at nine sports clubs and training centers across the West Bank, 470 (62.3%) reported previous wet-cupping use; 468 had sufficient primary-outcome data and were analyzed. Data were collected using a structured paper-based questionnaire incorporating the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Analyses included descriptive statistics, exact and chi-square tests, Spearman correlations, multiple linear regression, and path analysis. RESULTS: Improved mobility (30.8%), reduced muscle cramps (25.6%), enhanced immunity (16.2%), and increased endurance (9.0%) were the most frequently reported intended benefits. Cupping was commonly reported for chronic or recurrent conditions (99.6%), muscle strain (41.5%), and headaches (41.2%). Higher BMI and greater cupping-session frequency were associated with greater perceived cupping benefit (p = 0.010 and p < 0.001, respectively). Reported inflammation was associated with BMI category, gender, and competition level, while mild pain was associated with BMI category and competition level. Lower PSQI scores were associated with higher BMI, greater cupping-session frequency, and greater perceived cupping benefit. In the multivariable model, higher BMI, vitamin use, greater cupping-session frequency, greater perceived benefit, and manual rather than automated suction were independently associated with lower PSQI scores. The model explained 35.2% of the variance in sleep quality. CONCLUSION: Cupping-related practices and participant characteristics were associated with sleep quality. More frequent sessions, vitamin use, manual suction, higher BMI, and greater perceived benefit were associated with better sleep quality. These findings do not establish causality. Prospective studies are needed before cupping can be recommended to improve sleep or recovery.

metadata.title: Prevalence and predictors of in-class dozing among collegiate athletes and non-athletes.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Adequate sleep is critical for recovery and performance, yet athletes often experience less sleep than non-athletes, potentially impacting their academic performance. This study investigates the prevalence and factors in-class dozing among collegiate athletes compared to non-athletes. METHODS: This cross-sectional study surveyed 165 athletes and 92 non-athletes using an anonymous online questionnaire, focusing on sleep duration, commute times, part-time employment, and attitudes towards sleeping in class. RESULTS: Athletes reported a higher frequency of in-class dozing (70.4%) compared to non-athletes (55.5%, P=0.009). The primary reason for in-class dozing among athletes was fatigue from sports practice, whereas non-athletes attributed it to part-time work. Logistic regression analysis revealed that athletes had a higher risk of in-class dozing (OR=2.71, 95% CI 1.42-5.16, P=0.002), and both younger age (OR=0.46, 95% CI 0.24-0.87, P=0.016) and insufficient sleep at night (OR=0.71, 95% CI 0.55-0.92, P=0.010) were associated with increased risk. CONCLUSIONS: Both athletes and non-athletes are not obtaining adequate sleep, with athletes particularly affected by training-related fatigue possibly causing in-class dozing. Factors contributing to the likelihood of in-class dozing included younger age, inadequate nightly sleep, being an athlete, and engagement in part-time employment.

metadata.title: Longitudinal Serum Biomarker Profiles of Inflammation and Cartilage Matrix Metabolism During the First Year After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury initiates biological processes linked to joint tissue degeneration. The longitudinal time course of serum biomarkers reflecting inflammation and cartilage metabolism after ACL reconstruction (ACLR), particularly in comparison with uninjured controls, has not been characterized across the first postoperative year. HYPOTHESIS: Inflammatory (monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 [MCP-1]) and degradative (matrix metalloproteinase-3 [MMP-3]) biomarker concentrations would be elevated pre-ACLR and decrease over time, whereas cartilage turnover biomarker concentrations (cartilage oligomeric matrix protein [COMP] and type II collagen degradation-to-synthesis ratio [C2C:CPII]) would increase postoperatively. Also, pre-ACLR biomarker concentrations would be associated with concentrations at 6 and 12 months post-ACLR. STUDY DESIGN: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 2. METHODS: A total of 33 individuals with ACL injuries (52% female; mean age, 20.8 ± 2.4 years) were evaluated pre-ACLR and at 6 and 12 months post-ACLR. A total of 33 matched uninjured controls were included. Serum concentrations of MCP-1, MMP-3, COMP, and C2C:CPII were assessed using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Linear mixed-effects models with model-based contrasts were used to evaluate differences across groups and time points. ACLR-only linear mixed-effects regression models were used to assess associations between pre-ACLR and follow-up biomarker concentrations. Exploratory post hoc models evaluated differences by concomitant injury status. RESULTS: MCP-1 was elevated in individuals with ACL injuries compared with controls at all ACLR time points (all Padj < .001), with no change across ACLR time points. MMP-3 increased from pre-ACLR to 6 months post-ACLR (Padj < .001) but did not differ from controls at any time point. COMP was consistently greater in individuals with ACL injuries than in controls at all time points (all Padj≤ .021), with no changes across ACLR time points. C2C:CPII was greater at 12 months post-ACLR than at pre-ACLR and 6 months post-ACLR (both Padj < .001) and than in uninjured controls (Padj = .001). Pre-ACLR MCP-1, MMP-3, and COMP concentrations were associated with concentrations at both 6 and 12 months post-ACLR (all P≤ .006), whereas C2C:CPII was associated only with 12-month concentrations (P = .018). CONCLUSION: Inflammatory and cartilage-related biomarkers remain altered throughout the first year after ACLR, suggesting that the biological response is not fully resolved by reconstruction and standard rehabilitation but extends beyond the early postoperative period.

metadata.title: Baseline Performance and the 72-Hour Performance Window Following Plyometric Withdrawal in Collegiate Sprinters.
metadata.abstract: Plyometric studies emphasise pre-post change, but coaches need to know what remains after the block ends. This single-cohort study followed 26 collegiate sprinters through 12 weeks of Monday plyometric training and 4 weeks of withdrawal, without a parallel control group. During intervention, 30 m sprint time and arm-assisted countermovement jump (CMJ) height were measured at 0, 24, 48, 72, and 96 h; 0 and 72 h were retained during withdrawal. Mixed models showed large week effects for sprint, F(1, 1534) = 2272.01, partial η2 = 0.597, 95% CI [0.570, 0.622], and CMJ, F(1, 1534) = 2537.82, partial η2 = 0.623, 95% CI [0.598, 0.647]. Time-point effects were evident, but week × time-point interactions were not. Relative to 0 h, sprint was 0.0098 s slower at 24 h and 0.0057 s faster at 72 h; CMJ was 0.311 cm lower at 24 h and 0.245 cm higher at 72 h (all Tukey-adjusted p < 0.001). Linear, quadratic, and autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) models were compared by rolling one-step error. ARIMA had the lowest rolling errors and provided exploratory, model-based references for weeks 13-16. During withdrawal, 1/4 sprint and 0/4 CMJ 0 h observations fell within the 95% prediction interval; mean absolute deviations were 0.0233 s and 0.794 cm. Three of four 72 - 0 h observations were within the interval for both outcomes. The 72 - 0 h series more often fell within their model-based intervals than the 0 h series, indicating different short-term patterns.

metadata.title: Differential Splinting After Zone II Flexor Tendon Repair: The Bidirectional Splint.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Zone II flexor tendon injuries remain challenging because of the risks of rupture, adhesions, and stiffness. Splint design may influence repair-site tension during early healing. We describe a novel bidirectional splint (B-splint) that applies differential tensioning and compare its outcomes with those of conventional dorsal blocking splinting. METHODS: We retrospectively studied 59 patients (99 repaired tendons): 20 patients (31 tendons) treated with the B-splint after flexor digitorum profundus repair and 39 patients (68 tendons) treated with a dorsal blocking splint. The B-splint positions repaired digits in metacarpophalangeal flexion with interphalangeal extension while maintaining the noninjured digits in full extension. Functional outcomes were assessed using the modified Strickland score; tendon rupture and tenolysis were recorded. Categorical outcomes were compared using exact tests. RESULTS: No ruptures occurred in the B-splint cohort versus 1 in the control cohort. Excellent outcomes occurred in 19 of 20 B-splint patients (95%) versus 30 of 39 controls (77%), favoring the B-splint without statistical significance (P = 0.141). Tenolysis was less frequent with the B-splint (5% versus 13%). No B-splint patients developed stiffness of the noninjured digits. CONCLUSIONS: The B-splint was associated with favorable functional outcomes, no observed ruptures, and less tenolysis than conventional dorsal blocking splinting. It complements established rehabilitation strategies. Prospective studies are warranted to define its biomechanical and clinical role.

metadata.title: Athletes and Medical Staff in Elite Contact Sports: a Quantitative Analysis of Use, Knowledge, and Attitudes Regarding Cannabinoids.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cannabis use among elite contact sport athletes increases with legal reform and commercial availability. Limited education in cannabinoid pharmacology, use, and risk persists among athletes and medical staff, fostering stigma and reducing evidence-based guidance and communication. HYPOTHESIS: Athletes use cannabis but perceive stigma and discomfort discussing cannabis with medical staff. STUDY DESIGN: Quantitative, descriptive cross-sectional surveys. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 4. METHODS: Two anonymous online surveys were administered to elite and professional contact sport athletes (Canada, United States, Australia) and medical and training staff (February 2023 to July 2024). Descriptive statistics assessed demographics, use patterns, knowledge, education needs, attitudes, stigma, communication, and league policies. RESULTS: A total of 166 athletes (89.7% male, 35.2% aged 18-23 years) and 64 medical staff (physicians, athletic therapists, strength and conditioning coaches, etc) responded. Knowledge (pharmacology, interactions, dosing) was low. Overall, 56% of athletes currently used cannabinoids (81% having ever used), but only 21.7% knew the endocannabinoid system and 67.4% were unfamiliar with therapeutic dosing. Among medical staff, 59.5% were unfamiliar with mechanisms, only 14% were familiar with dosing protocols, and 71.4% lacked confidence in making treatment plans. Of the athletes, 86.5% believed cannabis had therapeutic value, 72.3% wanted education, and 74.1% favored qualified scientists as instructors. Of the medical staff, 79.5% reported strong educational need, with 100% of staff desiring athlete-specific cannabinoid education. Stigma and communication barriers were substantial: 81.3% of athletes perceived public stigma, 66.1% perceived staff stigma, and only 21.4% felt comfortable discussing cannabis with medical staff. Staff believed athletes would be honest if approached; however, <50% believed athletes trusted them enough to start the conversation. Both athletes and medical staff categorized cannabinoids as supplements or medications (unlike street drugs) and both supported legalization and a revision and update on league cannabis policies. CONCLUSION: Athletes and medical staff exhibit parallel knowledge gaps and strong educational needs amid high interest, use, and significant communication barriers. Evidence-informed education and stigma-reducing strategies are urgently needed. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Athletes increasingly use cannabinoids for pain, sleep, and recovery, while medical staff report insufficient training and low confidence. System-level education, communication, and policy updates may improve safety, decision-making, and trust.

metadata.title: Effects of Fatigue on Peak and Angle-Specific Hamstring-to-Quadriceps Ratios in Collegiate Women Lacrosse Athletes.
metadata.abstract: Background: Hamstring strains and anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears commonly occur in court and field sport athletes, with prevalence being higher in females. The likelihood of such injuries has been related to the hamstring-to-quadriceps (H:Q) strength ratio. Such a ratio can be affected by fatigue, to which athletes are frequently exposed. The aim of the current study was to investigate effects of fatigue on peak torque and angle-specific functional H:Q ratios at different angular velocities, as well as the association between resting functional H:Q ratios and those obtained following fatigue. Methods: A total of 18 collegiate women lacrosse players executed maximal knee concentric and eccentric contractions at angular velocities of 60, 180, and 240°/s following a supervised fatigue protocol. The isokinetic testing was then replicated. Results: There was a significant difference in functional peak torque H:Q ratios (p = 0.021-0.041) and ratios at 60 (p = 0.013-0.044), but not 20 degrees of knee flexion before and after fatigue at all three angular velocities. No main effects of angular velocity or ratio type were observed on H:Q ratio difference. The relationship between resting and fatigued functional H:Q ratios ranged from moderate to strong across all three angular velocities. Conclusions: Fatigue was associated with reductions in functional H:Q ratios, indicating altered knee flexor-extensor strength balance under fatigued conditions. In time-constrained settings, baseline functional H:Q ratio may provide practitioners with useful preliminary information regarding an athlete's potential susceptibility to lower-limb injury after fatigue.

metadata.title: Artificial intelligence across the continuum of care for the aging musculoskeletal patient: From longitudinal phenotyping to personalized surgery and recovery monitoring.
metadata.abstract: Musculoskeletal care is being reshaped by population aging, multimorbidity, frailty, osteoporosis, sarcopenia, polypharmacy and increasing vulnerability to postoperative loss of independence. Artificial intelligence (AI) has entered orthopaedic research, but its clinical translation remains constrained. Many models address isolated diagnostic, imaging or short-term prediction tasks rather than the longitudinal care trajectories that determine outcomes in older musculoskeletal patients. The central limitation is therefore not simply whether older adults are represented in datasets, but whether AI systems are valid across the continuum of geriatric orthopaedic care. This review argues for a transition from task-specific orthopaedic AI toward continuum-of-care AI for the aging musculoskeletal patient. Upstream, radiomics, longitudinal osteoarthritis phenotyping, opportunistic computed tomography (CT)-based skeletal assessment and AI-augmented dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) modelling may improve prediction of disease progression, fracture risk, treatment failure and surgical timing. At the point of intervention, AI-assisted arthroplasty planning may help move total knee arthroplasty from generic alignment targets toward phenotype-specific reconstruction strategies that account for constitutional alignment, bone morphology, ligament envelope, neuromuscular control, frailty and functional reserve. Perioperatively, automated frailty and sarcopenia phenotyping, wearable gait analysis and multimodal temporal models integrating imaging, electronic health records, laboratory data, medications, patient-reported outcomes and wearable signals may support dynamic risk prediction. After discharge, continuous monitoring of mobility, sleep, pain trajectories, wound-related symptoms and rehabilitation adherence may help close the high-risk surveillance gap during the 90-day postoperative episode. However, clinical adoption requires more than high discrimination. Explainable AI should be understood as one component of a broader trust framework that also includes calibration, uncertainty quantification, decision-curve analysis, external and prospective validation, workflow integration, post-deployment monitoring and accountability. The future of orthopaedic AI is not simply better diagnosis or more precise surgery, but longitudinal, multimodal support across the full care continuum: predicting progression, selecting treatment, personalizing surgery, optimizing perioperative care, monitoring recovery and preserving mobility and independence. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV.

metadata.title: Mapping evidence on kinesiophobia after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a scoping review.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This review identified, synthesized, and mapped the scientific evidence on kinesiophobia, as assessed by the Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia (TSK), in individuals following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), to provide clinicians with a comprehensive evidence map. INTRODUCTION: Kinesiophobia can negatively impact rehabilitation and return-to-sport outcomes after ACLR. Despite its clinical relevance, the available evidence is fragmented, making it challenging for clinicians to find clear answers to their clinical questions and apply findings consistently in practice. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We considered studies that assessed kinesiophobia using the TSK in individuals of any age or sex following ACLR, regardless of sport participation or geographical setting. Included sources comprised peer-reviewed primary and secondary research. METHODS: A comprehensive search was conducted in the PubMed, Scopus, Academic Search Ultimate (EBSCOhost), SPORTDiscus (EBSCOhost), CINAHL Plus (EBSCOhost), and MEDLINE (EBSCOhost) databases up to September 2025. Research alerts were then maintained throughout the review process to identify newly published studies. A framework synthesis approach was adopted, whereby studies were systematically charted across 10 thematic domains, reflecting how kinesiophobia has been investigated in ACLR. RESULTS: A total of 145 studies were included in this review. Most were cross-sectional and conducted in high-income countries, while longitudinal studies were limited. Adolescents and females were underrepresented, and the sample sizes and participant characteristics varied widely. Kinesiophobia was examined in relation to personal, clinical, functional, and neurophysiological variables. Intervention studies were scarce but explored cognitive-behavioral, educational, physical, and multimodal strategies for managing kinesiophobia. Only 2 studies adapted the TSK specifically for ACLR. CONCLUSIONS: Clinicians now have access to a structured map of the evidence on kinesiophobia post-ACLR, which may inform clinical reflection. Future research should address methodological limitations and expand investigations in underrepresented populations and contexts. REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://osf.io/dh4jk/JK.

metadata.title: Perineural Release with or Without Balloon Decompression for the Treatment of Lumbosacral Discogenic Syndromes in Professional Athletes.
metadata.abstract: Background: Lumbosacral discogenic syndrome (LSDS) is a common cause of low back pain (LBP) and lower limb pain (LLP) in athletes, often resulting in impaired sporting performance and delayed return to sport (RTS). Evidence regarding minimally invasive interventions, such as epidural perineural release (PNR), remains limited in athletic populations. Aim: This study aimed to compare outcomes following PNR with versus without balloon decompression neuroplasty in athletes with LSDS. Methods: We conducted a retrospective review of PNR performed between 2019 and 2024 for the treatment of LSDS among professional athletes. Demographic, clinical, and outcome data were collected from medical records and follow-up assessments. Pain intensity was assessed using the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), while patient-reported outcomes were evaluated using the EuroQoL-5D (EQ-5D). Additional outcomes included pain-free walking, standing, and sitting durations, and self-reported health scores. Results: A total of 33 patients who had one intervention were included. Significant improvements were observed in all pain, functional, and quality-of-life outcomes following treatment (all p < 0.001). Maximum, minimum, and average pain intensity decreased from 7.5 ± 1.7 to 2.8 ± 2.2, 3.8 ± 2.3 to 0.3 ± 0.7, and 5.6 ± 1.7 to 1.5 ± 1.2, respectively. All EQ-5D domains and quality of sleep also improved significantly (all p < 0.001). Pain-free walking, standing, and sitting durations increased significantly, from 24.8 ± 23.2 to 49.7 ± 26.7 min, 18.4 ± 20.0 to 44.1 ± 23.1 min, and 25.5 ± 23.7 to 44.6 ± 24.9 min, respectively (all p < 0.001). Self-reported health scores improved from 51.9 ± 22.6 to 83.0 ± 14.3 (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Epidural perineural release, with or without balloon decompression neuroplasty, was associated by significant improvements in pain, functional capacity, and quality of life among athletes with LSDS refractory to conservative management. These findings suggest that PNR may be a promising minimally invasive treatment option; however, controlled prospective studies are required to establish its effectiveness and determine the additional benefit of balloon decompression.

metadata.title: Biomechanical comparison of parallel versus convergent screw fixation in Zadek osteotomy.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: Zadek osteotomy is an increasingly utilized treatment for insertional Achilles tendinopathy (IAT), although an optimal fixation strategy remains unclear. This cadaveric study compared biomechanical outcomes of parallel and convergent screw fixation constructs following Zadek osteotomy. We hypothesized that convergent screw fixation would demonstrate greater stability. METHODS: Five paired fresh-frozen human calcanei (10 specimens) underwent simulated Zadek osteotomy, receiving paired parallel and convergent screw fixations on contralateral limbs. Specimens were tested using a servohydraulic system and motion tracking. Axial loading was applied until construct failure. Primary biomechanical outcomes included construct stiffness, load at 2 mm displacement, ultimate load to failure, and displacement at failure. Comparisons were performed using paired t-tests. One specimen was excluded from final analysis due to premature failure. RESULTS: No significant differences were observed between parallel and convergent constructs for any biomechanical outcome. Mean stiffness was 1415 ± 1337 N/mm for parallel constructs and 1360 ± 952 N/mm for convergent constructs (p = 0.96). Load at 2 mm displacement measured 707 ± 289 N and 892 ± 401 N, respectively (p = 0.54). Ultimate load to failure was 915 ± 266 N and 1065 ± 401 N, respectively (p = 0.55). Displacement at failure was similar between groups (p = 0.45). The combination shear-compression sliding at the osteotomy interface was the predominant mechanism of failure in both groups. CONCLUSION: Parallel and convergent screw constructs demonstrated comparable initial fixation strengths following Zadek osteotomy, suggesting screw trajectory may have limited impact on construct stability. Further studies are needed to validate these findings clinically.

metadata.title: Long-Term Failure Rate of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Using All-Inside 4-Stranded Semitendinosus Autograft Is 20.5.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate outcomes (graft failure, Patient-Reported Outcome Measures, and knee stability) after primary isolated anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction using the all-inside technique with 4-stranded semitendinosus autograft fixed between 2 adjustable-loop cortical suspension devices, with a minimum follow-up of 10 years. METHODS: Patients who underwent primary isolated ACL reconstruction using the all-inside 4-stranded semitendinosus between January 2011 and January 2013, with a minimum of 10-year follow-up, were included. Patients completed a standardized questionnaire and were offered a follow-up consultation. The questionnaire included the Tegner, ACL-Return to Sport after Injury, Subjective Knee Value, subjective International Knee Documentation Committee, and assessment of graft failure. Clinical evaluations and laxity measurements were conducted during follow-up consultations. RESULTS: At a mean follow-up of 138 months (range: 122-159), 156 patients completed the questionnaire, and 111 were clinically evaluated. The mean age was 39.6 ± 9.7 years (range: 15-62). Graft failure occurred in 20.5% of cases (32/156). The mean decrease in Tegner was 1.03 ± 1.23 points, and 51% returned to their preinjury sport level. The median preoperative Tegner was 7.0 (interquartile range: 6.0-7.0). A higher preoperative Tegner was associated with an increased risk of graft failure (P = .016). Graft failure occurred in 23% of males and 16.6% of females (P = .461). Patients with grafts sized ≤8 mm (n = 85) had a failure rate of 17.5%, compared with 23.9% for grafts >8 mm (P = .441). The mean subjective International Knee Documentation Committee was 85.6 ± 13.5, Subjective Knee Value 79.2 ± 22.1, and ACL-Return to Sport after Injury 69.5 ± 26.5. Among patients without reported graft failure, 16.5% exhibited >3 mm differential anterior laxity, and 28% had a pivot-shift score ≥2. CONCLUSIONS: At a minimum 10-year follow-up, primary isolated ACL reconstruction using an all-inside 4-stranded semitendinosus autograft showed a 20.5% graft failure rate, despite favorable patient-reported outcomes. A higher preoperative Tegner showed a trend toward increased graft failure. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, retrospective case series.
