metadata.title: Bone Mineral Density in Physique-Focused and Non-Physique-Focused Female Collegiate Athletes: Associations With Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport Risk Factors.
metadata.abstract: Kolb, DE, Cipriano, NL, Moody, RA, Stephens, JA, Caldwell, LK, Lindley, MR, Ware, ME, and Deemer, SE. Bone mineral density in physique-focused and non-physique-focused female collegiate athletes: Associations with relative energy deficiency in sport risk factors. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Bone mineral density (BMD) is a critical indicator of skeletal health and long-term injury risk in athletic populations. Female athletes are susceptible to changes in BMD because of sport-specific training demands, hormonal dysregulation, and energy availability. The present study aimed to compare BMD between physique-focused (PF; endurance, aesthetic, and weight-dependent sports) and non-physique-focused (NPF; ball, power, and skill-based sports) female collegiate athletes and assess risk factors associated with relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) across both groups. Thirty-three female athletes were evaluated for BMD by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), REDs risk using the Clinical Assessment Tool 2 (CAT2), anthropometric measurements, blood biomarkers, the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q), and the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q). Group differences were assessed using independent t-tests with significance set at p < 0.05. Physique-focused athletes demonstrated significantly lower DXA-derived z-scores at anteroposterior spine, right and left femur, and total body sites than NPF athletes (p < 0.001). There were no differences in leptin (p = 0.35), cortisol (p = 0.16), vitamin D (p = 0.29), LEAF-Q total score (p = 0.72), or global EDE-Q score (p = 0.10). No group differences in CAT2 REDs risk were observed; thus, subjects were combined: 19 athletes were classified as "green;" 12 were "yellow;" and 2 were "orange." Lower BMD in PF athletes supports the importance of early screening and targeted interventions to support bone health. These findings suggest sport type may influence skeletal outcomes independent of traditional REDs indicators, emphasizing the need for sport-specific assessment strategies.

metadata.title: Consumer Grade Wearable Sensor Metrics Are Associated with Internal Forces at Common Running Injury Locations.
metadata.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Inexpensive consumer-grade wearable sensors have expanded possibilities to assess, monitor, or modify a runner's gait. However, it is unclear which sensor-measured gait metrics are strongly associated with internal loading at common injury locations. PURPOSE: To measure the association between gait metrics measured by consumer-grade wearable sensors and internal forces at the Achilles tendon and the patellofemoral joint. METHODS: 55 healthy runners wearing consumer-grade chest straps foot-pods completed a 38-minute run on an instrumented treadmill at 12 speeds from 70%-125% of self-reported typical running pace. A scaled musculoskeletal model derived from motion capture data and driven by static optimization was used to calculate Achilles tendon and patellofemoral joint forces during stance for each speed. Functional regression models were used to estimate the associations of each of nine sensor-measured gait metrics with internal forces across stance, after adjusting for body mass and running speed. RESULTS: At both the Achilles tendon and the patellofemoral joint, cadence, vertical oscillation, and vertical ratio (vertical oscillation divided by step length) showed the strongest associations with internal forces (maximum of 0.4-0.6 BW change in force per one standard deviation change in the gait metric). Other wearable sensor-measured gait metrics, including stance time, leg stiffness, and stance time percent showed weaker associations (<0.4 BW change in force per one standard deviation change in the gait metric). CONCLUSIONS: Runners with higher-than-average cadence, vertical oscillation, or vertical ratio values experience marked differences in internal forces at the Achilles tendon and patellofemoral joint. Of these gait metrics, cadence is the most practical for out-of-lab use because of its ease of accurate measurement with consumer-grade devices.

metadata.title: Do Athletes Lose Soleus Strength Over the Course of a Season? Longitudinal Monitoring of Seated Plantar Flexion Maximum Voluntary Contraction Strength and Factors That Affect It in Australian Football Players.
metadata.abstract: Green, B, Pizzari, T, Schache, AG, Rio, EK, Evans, SCS, Cooper, S, and Murphy, MC. Do athletes lose soleus strength over the course of a season? Longitudinal monitoring of seated plantar flexion maximum voluntary contraction strength and factors that affect it in Australian football players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The calf muscles are critical to dynamic lower-limb function in sports but are susceptible to injury. Despite its role in performance and injury, research has not evaluated soleus strength changes over the course of a season, or factors affecting it. Flexed-knee maximum plantar flexion strength was longitudinally monitored in state-league Australian footballers (2 Western Australian and 1 Victorian team) across 1-season at timepoints: preseason (T0), early in-season (T1), late in-season (T2). Generalized estimating equations evaluated strength outcomes over time (absolute, relative, asymmetry). Intrinsic factors (e.g., age, sex, injury history, sport exposure history, calf-focused resistance training) were analyzed to determine longitudinal associations with strength. Forty-one athletes (32 male, 9 female) were monitored across 210 strength measurements from T0 to T2. Absolute (T0 = 121.7 ± 27 kg; T1 = 135.2 ± 27.3 kg; T2 = 135.8 ± 25.9 kg) and relative (T0 = 1.51 ± 0.28 body mass [BM]; T1 = 1.69 ± 0.27 BM, T2 = 1.75 ± 0.26 BM) strength demonstrated longitudinal change (absolute: β = 19.33 kg, relative: β = 0.24 BM; p < 0.001). Reduced strength was associated with a recent calf injury history (relative and absolute: p < 0.001) and older age (p = 0.03). Lower strength (absolute: β = -23.53 kg, relative: β = -0.22 BM; p < 0.05) and larger asymmetry (β = 8.13 kg, p = 0.01) were detected in female athletes. Athletes can be expected to improve and maintain soleus capacity across seasonal periods. Athlete age, calf injury history, and sex can affect strength longitudinally. These findings may guide individualized prevention, performance, and postinjury benchmarking.

metadata.title: All-Suture Fixation for Acute Turf Toe Injuries.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Turf toe is a hallux metatarsophalangeal joint (MTPJ) injury caused by hyperextension of the great toe with axial loading1,2. High-grade injuries may threaten return to sport and require surgery3,4. Here, we describe a capsular reconstruction of the great toe MTPJ with all-knotless suture anchors and suture tape augmentation for turf toe injuries, in isolation or in combination with a traumatic bunion, designed to reduce suture burden, minimize soft-tissue irritation, and facilitate recovery. DESCRIPTION: The procedure begins with the patient supine. A direct medial approach to the hallux MTPJ is performed. Both the medial base of the proximal phalanx and the medial eminence of the metatarsal head are drilled at isometric points, and augmentation with suture tape is then performed. Isometric drill holes are placed in the medial proximal phalanx base and metatarsal head for suture tape augmentation. A knotless suture anchor is placed approximately 3 mm proximal to the articular margin of the metatarsal head, repairing the medial capsule in a horizontal mattress fashion. An additional knotless anchor is placed at the plantar plate insertion, and the suture is passed through the tibial sesamoid sling and tensioned with the toe in 20° of plantar flexion. Suture tape is secured into the proximal phalanx with an interference screw, then passed through the deep capsule into the metatarsal head, followed by the placement of an additional interference screw into the metatarsal head. The anchor is inserted into the plantar-medial proximal phalanx at the flexor hallucis brevis insertion. The toe is flexed during tensioning, then adjusted per clinical examination and the sesamoid location beneath the metatarsal head. Knotless fixation permits incremental tensioning with intraoperative assessment of motion. Final tensioning is performed with the toe in neutral to correct deformity without overconstraint, preserving range of motion. ALTERNATIVES: Nonoperative alternatives include rest, ice, compression and elevation; anti-inflammatory drugs; activity modification; and brief immobilization5,6. Operative alternatives include primary capsuloligamentous complex repair with nonabsorbable sutures, plantar plate advancement with bone tunnels or suture anchors if primary repair is not feasible, and concomitant procedures such as sesamoidectomy and bunionectomy based on the injury pattern2,7,8. RATIONALE: This technique is intended for high-grade turf toe injuries with capsuloligamentous disruption, sesamoid complex insufficiency, and MTPJ instability. Nonoperative treatment may be appropriate in cases of low-grade injury; however, persistent pain, instability, or loss of push-off strength following nonoperative treatment would indicate a higher-grade injury. Compared with isolated repair or plantar plate advancement alone, this technique restores both static and dynamic stabilizers of the hallux MTPJ while addressing associated angular deformity. Suture tape augmentation resists recurrent hyperextension and valgus forces while allowing controlled physiologic motion. Knotless, low-profile suture anchors minimize bulk and hardware prominence in a region with limited soft-tissue coverage and bone stock. This construct offers a robust reconstruction option for athletes requiring predictable restoration of stability and reliable return to sport. EXPECTED OUTCOMES: Operative treatment of high-grade turf toe injuries has been shown to result in reliable pain relief, restored stability, and high rates of return to sport8. Previous studies have suggested improved function and earlier return to play compared with prolonged nonoperative treatment in appropriate patients6,7. Knotless suture anchors reduce implant prominence and eliminate knot-related irritation, while the small insertional diameter of the suture anchors preserves bone stock in the metatarsal head and proximal phalanx. This construct provides immediate stability while allowing controlled motion, facilitating rehabilitation, and reducing postoperative stiffness. Athletes typically return to unrestricted activity within 6 to 9 months, aided by the suture tape augmentation allowing earlier movement through the range of motion. This augmentation reduces the need for long-term spica splinting and bracing and reduces the risk of recurrence. IMPORTANT TIPS: The small anchor diameter and use of suture tape allow easy access without hardware burden.○ Suture choice depends on surgeon preference regarding construct stiffness and on the tissue quality and risk of irritation. We believe that suture tape lays flatter and, if required, knots are smaller.Avoid suture twisting or kinking, which can prematurely lock anchors, compromising fixation.○ After the anchor is placed, we keep the suture tape secured out of the field as we prepare the capsule with absorbable suture. As we load the second anchor, we maintain tension on the tape to prevent twisting.Overtightening the MTPJ capsule may lead to altered biomechanics. ACRONYMS AND ABBREVIATIONS: RICE = rest, ice, compression, elevationMRI = magnetic resonance imagingBID = twice daily.

metadata.title: Bony Anatomy, Soft-Tissue Adaptations and Neuromuscular Risk Factors of Shoulder Injury in Handball Players: A Narrative Review.
metadata.abstract: Handball is a high-intensity contact sport that imposes significant mechanical stress on the shoulder joint through repetitive, high-velocity overhead throwing, predisposing athletes to a wide spectrum of shoulder injuries. This narrative review examines the factors associated with shoulder injuries in handball players, highlighting underlying structural, adaptive and functional mechanisms across male and female athletes. A literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE was conducted to synthesize current evidence on bony anatomy, soft tissue adaptations and neuromuscular characteristics in handball cohorts. Factors associated with shoulder injury or symptoms can be broadly categorized into three conceptual domains: (i) bony anatomy and structural features, (ii) soft tissue adaptations and (iii) dynamic functional and neuromuscular factors. Bony factors include reduced acromiohumeral distance, increased humeral retrotorsion as a sport-specific skeletal adaptation and variations in glenoid morphology that may influence glenohumeral stability. Soft tissue adaptations include posterior capsular tightness, anterior capsular laxity and alterations in shoulder range of motion, particularly glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD) accompanied by external rotation gain (ERG), which may influence glenohumeral kinematics and potentially contribute to shoulder symptoms or overuse conditions. Beyond these structural features, dynamic functional factors, including shoulder rotator muscle strength imbalances, impaired scapular control and training-load management, play a central role in injury development. Therefore, a comprehensive assessment encompassing anatomical correlates, soft tissue characteristics and functional/neuromuscular characteristics may support the development of targeted injury-prevention and rehabilitation strategies in handball players.

metadata.title: Multi-Modal Biometric Fusion for Athletic Performance Optimization: Clinical Validation of the Dynamic Multi-Sensor Fusion Classifier (DMSFC).
metadata.abstract: Integrating real-time biometric monitoring into sports science is increasingly important for optimizing athletic performance and reducing injury risk. However, many existing systems have limited capacity to accurately combine data from multiple biometric sources. This study evaluated the Dynamic Multisensor Fusion (DMSFC) classifier for analyzing physiological and functional data collected from multiple biometric modalities, including electrocardiography (ECG), fingerprint measurements, and facial recognition. A multimodal biometric framework based on DMSFC was developed to monitor and classify key health and performance indicators in elite athletes. The variables evaluated included heart rate (HR), oxygen saturation (SpO₂), blood pressure (BP), flexibility, muscle strength, and endurance capacity. The performance of the classifier was evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). After implementing the proposed monitoring framework, improvements were observed in the evaluated performance and health indicators. The mean heart rate decreased from 78 to 66 beats per minute, while oxygen saturation slightly increased from 98% to 99%. Blood pressure decreased from 120/80 mmHg to 110/70 mmHg. Flexibility improved from 32 to 36 cm, muscle strength increased from 105 to 122 pounds, and endurance capacity increased from 20 to 24 minutes. Among the evaluated classifiers, DMSFC showed a strongest overall performance (i.e., accuracy of 0.94, sensitivity of 0.91, specificity of 0.96, and AUC of 0.97). These findings suggest that DMSFC could be capable of providing an effective framework for multimodal biometric analysis in sports science. Its use may support athlete assessment, facilitate the development of individualized training programs, and contribute to injury prevention strategies. Because the reported physiological changes were observed after implementation of the framework, further controlled studies are needed to determine whether they were caused by the monitoring system, the associated exercise program, or other factors.

metadata.title: Nonoperative Management of an Acute Complete Achilles Tendon Rupture With Mesenchymal Stem Cells and Extracellular Vesicles: A Case Report.
metadata.abstract: An acute complete rupture of the Achilles tendon with a large intertendinous gap is conventionally regarded as a surgical indication, yet operative repair carries a significant burden on wound-healing and potential for neurovascular complications, whereas nonoperative care may be limited by re-rupture and incomplete functional recovery. Human umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (hUC-MSCs) and their secreted extracellular vesicles (EVs) exert immunomodulatory, pro-angiogenic and pro-tenogenic paracrine effects that could support tendon healing. A healthy 45-year-old recreationally active male sustained an acute complete rupture of the right Achilles tendon while playing tennis. A 3.0-T magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed a full-thickness mid-substance rupture located 6.1 cm proximal to the calcaneal insertion, with a 3.7 cm gap. He delayed treatment and opted out of surgical management and was offered nonoperative care with a combined biologic regimen: two ultrasound-guided intralesional injections of hUC-MSC-derived EVs (a total of 30 × 10⁹ vesicles) deposited into the tendon gap, both stumps, and the peritendon along with three consecutive daily intravenous (IV) infusions of hUC-MSCs (approximately 1.7 × 10⁶ cells/kg of total body weight) as a paracrine priming adjuvant, alongside an injury-guided functional rehabilitation program. Pain measured using the numeric rating scale (NRS) decreased from 10/10 at baseline to 0/10 at six months post-intervention. At final follow-up (approx 14 months) the patient had returned to regular weight training and jogging without pain or functional limitations. On physical examination, the Thompson Test was negative, the Achilles Tendon Total Rupture Score (ATRS) and the American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society (AOFAS) ankle-hindfoot scores were both calculated as 100/100, and instrumented biomechanical testing showed near-symmetric lower-limb range of motion and balance. Follow-up MRI demonstrated a remodeled tendon with restoration of continuity and no residual gap. No mild or severe adverse events were reported during or after procedures. In this single case report, a combined regimen of systemic hUC-MSCs and intralesional hUC-MSC-derived EVs was associated with imaging-confirmed tendon healing and full functional recovery of an acute complete Achilles tendon rupture managed nonoperatively. This treatment protocol serves as a hypothesis-generating observation with potential for validation in controlled prospective studies.

metadata.title: Spaceflight human optimization and performance: positioning astronauts in an operational framework to promote health, fitness, and mission readiness.
metadata.abstract: Optimizing astronaut mission readiness is a multidisciplinary endeavor that should integrate concepts from aerospace medicine, human performance, sports science, nutrition, and engineering. Situating astronauts within a theoretical framework similar to that of operational athletes, while addressing top human systems capability needs outlined for future missions, may be optimal for promoting sustained health and performance before, during, and after missions to low-Earth orbit, the lunar surface, and Mars. Mission readiness can be optimized by enhancing physiological and behavioral/psychological performance through data-driven and individualized exercise countermeasures, health and performance monitoring, precision nutrition, and rehabilitation strategies. Appropriate and stable space food systems that facilitate adequate provision of nutrients and fluids to prime astronauts for mission-critical tasks and operational demands are needed, though research is needed into potential nutritional considerations that might be useful for future missions. Behavioral readiness programs should emphasize stress inoculation, adaptive decision-making, communication, Earth-independent operation functionality, conflict resolution, leadership, and team-based problem-solving before flight to promote healthy team dynamics in-flight, along with proper society reintegration and uptake of family and occupational roles post-flight. Exercise remains an essential countermeasure during spaceflight, with an emphasis on maximizing fitness before launch to mitigate in-flight declines and on maintaining fitness levels and functionality during flight through high-intensity multimodal exercise. Following return to Earth, rehabilitative programs serve to restore cardiovascular, sensorimotor, and skeletal function, followed by enhancing skill-based performance components through a phase-based training program. Continuous monitoring systems that provide insight into health, performance, sleep, cognitive, nutritional, and recovery status should enable data-driven decision-making on physical readiness across all mission phases. By integrating insight from multiple disciplines, this unifying approach delivers a theoretical framework for sustaining astronaut health and performance during extended-duration missions.

metadata.title: Female Versus Male Differences in Burnout With Sport: A Systematic Review.
metadata.abstract: CONTEXT: Burnout is a widely recognized problem in sports. Female athletes have been found to experience more emotional exhaustion and less depersonalization, key components of burnout, than their male counterparts. Researchers have found varied results when comparing rates of burnout between male and female athletes. OBJECTIVE: This study aims to review the current literature with the goal of determining what differences exist between male and female athletes regarding sport burnout. DATA SOURCES: PubMed (Medline), Cochrane library, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL, Embase, and Web of Science. STUDY SELECTION: Articles that were originally written in English, included athletes participating in organized sport, evaluated athletic burnout, and compared rates of burnout among different sexes were included in this review. Articles that were cadaveric, animal, review, or expert opinions were excluded. STUDY DESIGN: Systematic review. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 4. DATA EXTRACTION: The age, sex, sport, and level of athletic competition of individual athletes were extracted from each article in addition to burnout rates and outcome scores of male and female athletes. RESULTS: Of the 18 studies included in this review, 10 (56%) found no significant differences in sport burnout among male and female athletes, 7 (39%) found that female athletes experienced greater burnout than male athletes and 1 (5.6%) found that male athletes experienced greater burnout than female athletes. Reduced sense of accomplishment and physical/emotional exhaustion were implicated in creating more burnout among female athletes than their male counterparts in 4 studies. CONCLUSION: It remains unclear how the constructs of sex and gender affect athlete burnout. The heterogeneity of studies included in this review prevented the analysis of how participation in team sports, participation in individual sports, level of competition, and the coach-athlete relationship influence sport burnout. More standardized studies are needed to better evaluate the effect sex and gender have on athlete burnout as well as how athletes involved in various sports are affected by burnout.

metadata.title: Sleep Quality and Sleep Timing in Adolescent Gymnasts: A Cross-Sectional Study.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Given the limited pediatric-specific evidence in this area, we aimed to examine the association between federated-level gymnastics participation and sleep quality and sleep timing in adolescents. The global Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) score was defined as the primary outcome, sleep-timing measures as secondary outcomes, and individual PSQI component analyses as exploratory. METHODS: This observational, cross-sectional comparative study included adolescents aged 12 to 16 years participating in federated gymnastics and controls who did not participate in federated sports. Demographic variables included age, sex, and parental educational level, while training-related variables included weekly training duration, number of training sessions, and training schedule. Sleep quality was assessed using the PSQI, and bedtime, wake-up time, sleep duration, and sleep latency were derived from the corresponding PSQI items. Multiple linear regression models included age, sex, maternal educational level, and paternal educational level as covariates. RESULTS: The study included 60 gymnasts and 37 controls, with baseline differences in age, sex distribution, and parental educational level between groups. Gymnasts trained a median of 12.0 hours/week (Q1-Q3: 8.25 to 20.0) over five sessions/week (Q1-Q3: 4 to 6), with a median training-session end time of 20:30 (range: 18:00 to 22:00). In adjusted analyses, gymnast status was associated with later bedtime (B=0.392 hours, 95% CI 0.043 to 0.740, p=0.028), whereas no statistically significant association was observed between study group and global PSQI score (B=0.311, 95% CI -0.720 to 1.343, p=0.550). Increasing age was associated with later bedtime (B=0.231 hours, p=0.004) and shorter sleep duration (B=-0.398 hours, 95% CI -0.560 to -0.236, p<0.001). Among gymnasts, training-session end time was not associated with global PSQI score (B=0.141, 95% CI -0.344 to 0.625, p=0.563; R²=0.006). Overall, 19/97 participants (19.6%) met the conventional PSQI >5 threshold for poor sleep quality, although an optimal adolescent-specific clinical cutoff has not been definitively established. CONCLUSION: No statistically significant difference in adjusted global PSQI score was detected between federated adolescent gymnasts and controls. Gymnast status was associated with later bedtime. Approximately one in five participants met the conventional PSQI >5 threshold for poor sleep quality. Given the cross-sectional design, these findings should be interpreted as associations, and larger longitudinal studies incorporating objective sleep measures are warranted.

metadata.title: Acute Sodium Bicarbonate Supplementation Enhances 10-km Outdoor Track Running Performance in Recreational Female Runners.
metadata.abstract: This study investigated the effects of acute sodium bicarbonate (SB) supplementation co-ingested with a carbohydrate-rich meal on 10-km running performance and gastrointestinal symptoms in recreational female runners under field-based conditions. Twenty-one healthy women (33.6 ± 4.6 years; body mass index 20.8 ± 1.3 kg/m; maximal oxygen uptake 48.6 ± 2.0 ml·kg-1·min-1) completed two 10-km outdoor track running time trials (TTs) in a randomized, double-blind, crossover design. Participants ingested either SB (0.3 g/kg body mass [BM]) or placebo (PLA; 0.03 g/kg BM table salt), together with a standardized carbohydrate-rich meal (1.5 g/kg BM), 90 min before exercise during the same phase of the menstrual cycle. Blood pH, bicarbonate [HCO3-], and [lactate] were measured before, and 1, 3, 5, and 7 min after the TTs; performance time was recorded. Gastrointestinal symptoms were recorded at 30, 60, and 90 min after SB and PLA ingestions. Blood pH (7.47 ± 0.03 vs. 7.42 ± 0.04, p < .001) and [HCO3-] (27.7 ± 1.4 vs. 22.2 ± 1.5 mmol/L, p < .001) were higher at rest and remained elevated postexercise following SB compared with PLA (p < .05 for all time points). TT completion time improved after SB compared with PLA (3,046.1 ± 208.7 s vs. 3,078.4 ± 206.8 s; p = .011). No significant differences in gastrointestinal symptoms scores were observed between conditions (p > .05 for all). In conclusion, acute co-ingestion of 0.3 g/kg of SB with a carbohydrate-rich meal is a practical and well-tolerated strategy to achieve higher resting blood [HCO3-] and pH as well as to improve 10-km TT running performance in recreational female runners.

metadata.title: Physical examination of the cervical spine should be conducted in female athletes with a history of concussion.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Female athletes may be at increased risk of injury following sports-related concussion (SRC), even after symptom resolution. Residual cervical spine impairments have been proposed as a potential contributor; however, these have not been well characterised in female athletes. This study aimed to examine whether a history of SRC was associated with clinical assessments of the cervical spine in female athletes. METHODS: In this cross-sectional observational study, 156 elite and pre-elite female athletes from water polo, soccer, diving, rugby-7s and cycling/BMX were recruited. History of SRC within the previous 12 months was self-reported. Assessments included questionnaires and physical examination of the cervical spine, comprising range of motion, manual examination, joint position error (JPE) and maximal isometric neck strength. Between-group differences were examined using univariable statistical analyses. RESULTS: Athletes with a history of SRC demonstrated a higher prevalence of reduced cervical range of motion, positive findings on manual examination, increased JPE and a history of headaches or migraines compared with athletes without concussion history. No deficits in maximal isometric neck strength were observed in athletes with a history of SRC. CONCLUSION: Cervical spine impairments were more commonly observed in female athletes with a history of SRC within the previous 12 months, including in athletes who did not report current neck pain. These findings suggest consideration of targeted cervical spine assessment beyond symptom-based screening in athletes with a concussion history. Whether identification and management of cervical spine impairments influence subsequent injury risk requires investigation in prospective and interventional studies.

metadata.title: Endocrine dynamics of special operations forces across mission cycles: implications for human stress physiology.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: This study investigates the endocrine responses and muscle damage markers in elite male Special Operations Force operators across operational phases to understand hormonal adaptations to extreme operational stress and recovery. METHODS: Fifty-six operators (28-42 years) participated in a longitudinal study conducted at a Special Operations Forces unit. Blood samples were collected at three visits: Visit 1 (baseline recovery), Visit 2 (intensive pre-deployment training), and Visit 3 (post-deployment recovery). Serum concentrations of testosterone (T), cortisol (CORT), dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S), growth hormone (GH), insulin-like growth factor-I (IGF-I), progesterone (P4), creatine kinase (CK), and myoglobin (Mb) were analyzed. RESULTS: Post-deployment (Visit 3), T levels increased (+ 20%, p < 0.05), and CORT decreased (- 23%, p < 0.05), resulting in a significantly higher testosterone-to-cortisol ratio compared with Visit 1 and Visit 2 (p ≤ 0.05). DHEA-S correlated with CORT (r = 0.37, p < 0.05), suggesting a compensatory adrenal response under stress. GH concentrations were markedly reduced post-deployment (- 84%, p ≤ 0.05), while IGF-I remained stable, indicating differential regulation within the GH-IGF-I axis during recovery. P4 concentrations remained elevated across all phases, reflecting a consistent endocrine feature across operational phases rather than a defined mechanistic adaptation. No significant changes were observed in CK or Mb, underscoring effective physical stress management at the time of post-deployment sampling. CONCLUSION: These findings emphasize the importance of tailored training and recovery strategies for sustaining endocrine balance, resilience, and operational readiness in elite military personnel.

metadata.title: Sleep Characteristics of Elite Female Soccer Players Competing in the National Women's Soccer League Across a Competitive Season.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: Sleep supports recovery and readiness in professional sport, yet season-long objective data in women's professional soccer are limited. This study aimed to provide a longitudinal, objective description of sleep across a competitive season and to compare sleep characteristics between preseason and in-season phases. METHODS: Twenty-seven professional athletes were monitored from January to November 2024 using a finger-worn wearable. Nightly total sleep time (TST), sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency (SOL), and sleep stage durations were extracted. Preseason versus in-season differences were examined using linear mixed-effects models and reported as estimated marginal mean differences with 95% CIs. RESULTS: During the in-season, TST averaged 7.8 (1.2) hours (median: 7.9 h), sleep efficiency 89.1% (5.4%), and SOL 15.6 (12.6) minutes. Mean sleep stage durations were 262.8 (52.8) minutes (light), 96.6 (31.8) minutes (deep), and 106.8 (34.2) minutes (Rapid Eye Movement). Notable night-to-night variability was observed, particularly for TST (within-player coefficients of variation: 10%-18%) and SOL (50%-114%). Compared with preseason, in-season sleep was characterized by lower REM sleep (-4.8 min, 95% CI -6.9 to -2.8; P < .001), reduced sleep efficiency (-0.37%, 95% CI -0.71 to -0.02; P = .036), and shorter SOL (-1.1 min, 95% CI -2.0 to -0.2; P = .020). TST did not differ between phases (P = .287), and deep and light sleep remained unchanged. Effect sizes were small (Cohen d ≤ 0.15). CONCLUSIONS: Group averages of sleep parameters might mask individual and seasonal changes in sleep, highlighting the need for longitudinal, athlete-specific monitoring to guide proactive sleep monitoring strategies.

metadata.title: Greater weapon-side supraspinatus tendon thickness in elite national-team fencers: an exploratory cross-sectional ultrasound study.
metadata.abstract: Fencing exposes the weapon arm to repetitive loading that differs from conventional overhead sports, yet shoulder morphology in elite fencers is poorly described. We compared supraspinatus tendon thickness, resting acromiohumeral distance (AHD), and occupation ratio between shoulders in 15 elite national-team fencers without current shoulder pain during daily life or competition. Bilateral ultrasonography measured tendon thickness at 5 and 10 mm lateral to the biceps tendon in the modified Crass position. Mean tendon thickness was greater on the weapon side (5.37 ± 0.89 vs 4.67 ± 0.96 mm; mean difference, 0.70 mm; 95% CI, 0.30 to 1.11; p = 0.002), with the difference most evident at 5 mm. No statistically significant between-side difference in resting AHD was detected (p = 0.085), whereas occupation ratio was higher on the weapon side (p = 0.013). Our findings suggest that fencers' shoulders can differ in structure even when neither side is painful. This is worth remembering when the opposite shoulder is used as an ultrasound reference, although the cause and clinical relevance of the difference are not yet known.

metadata.title: Five-Year Outcomes and Return to Sport After Arthroscopic Bankart Repair in Young Patients With Minimal (<10%) or No Glenoid Bone Loss.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Arthroscopic Bankart repair is commonly used to address anterior instability in adolescents and young adults with no or minimal bone loss. However, failure rates remain high, particularly in high-risk populations. PURPOSE/HYPOTHESIS: The purpose of this study was to evaluate clinical outcomes, return-to-sport (RTS) rates, and predictors of failure after arthroscopic Bankart repair in patients ≤24 years of age with minimal glenoid bone loss. It was hypothesized that patients would demonstrate favorable outcomes, low recurrence rates, and high RTS rates, and smaller distance-to-dislocation (DTD) measurements, and contact sports participation would be associated with failure. STUDY DESIGN: Case series; Level of evidence, 4. METHODS: The data of patients with anterior shoulder instability and minimal bone loss (<10%) who underwent primary arthroscopic Bankart repair between 2006 and 2020 were retrospectively analyzed. Remplissage was not performed. Data collected included preoperative instability events, patient-reported outcome measures, satisfaction, radiographic measurements (glenoid bone loss, glenoid track, and DTD), and RTS outcomes. Failure was defined as re-dislocation or recurrent instability requiring surgery. RESULTS: A total of 130 patients were evaluated; 18 were excluded, leaving 112. Of these, 96 patients (85.7%) were available for the final follow-up (mean age, 19.9 ± 3.1 years; mean follow-up, 68.4 ± 42.7 months). All clinical outcomes improved significantly (P < .05) except for the 12-Item Short Form Health Survey Mental Component Summary score. The median satisfaction score was 9 (IQR, 8-10). Participation in contact sports was associated with failure, while other risk factors were not. RTS was achieved by 96.1% of patients; however, only 57.1% returned to their preinjury level. Fewer preoperative dislocation events were associated with successful return to full activity (P = .04). The recurrence rate was 33.3%, and revision surgery was required in 19 patients (19.8%). CONCLUSION: Arthroscopic Bankart repair was associated with high rates of recurrence and revision surgery in a series of patients ≤24 years of age without glenoid bone loss. In those who did not require revision surgery, clinical outcomes and RTS rates were high. Contact sports participation was associated with failure. A greater number of preoperative instability events negatively influence RTS outcomes. Arthroscopic Bankart repair in this population is safe and has a low complication rate, but the failure rate remains considerable.

metadata.title: Validity of triaxial accelerometer for estimating total energy expenditure in elite female university athletes: a doubly labeled water study.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Accurate estimation of total energy expenditure (TEE) in athletes is essential for determining energy requirements to support training, recovery, and performance. Basal metabolic rate (BMR) is one of the key components associated with the accuracy of TEE estimation. However, few studies have evaluated the accuracy of BMR and TEE estimation methods in athletic populations. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to examine the validity of the Cunningham equation for BMR estimation and the accelerometer-based method (ACCTRI) for TEE estimation in elite female university runners, using the doubly labeled water (DLW) method as the reference criterion. METHODS: We analyzed data from 16 elite female university runners (mean age 20 ± 1 years). We assessed: (1) the association and agreement between BMR estimated using the Cunningham equation and BMR measured by indirect calorimetry, and (2) the association and agreement between TEE estimated using the ACCTRI method and TEE measured using the DLW method. RESULTS: Correlational analysis revealed significant, positive, and strong associations between estimated and measured BMR (r = 0.728, P = 0.001) and between estimated and measured TEE (r = 0.828, P = 0.001). Bland-Altman analyses showed good agreement between estimated and measured BMR (bias, ~1.6%). The mean TEE difference between two method was 416 ± 242 kcal/day. CONCLUSIONS: The Cunningham equation provides reasonably accurate estimates of BMR. ACCTRI overestimated TEE by approximately 12% compared to DLW, thus support staff should consider this when supporting female runners.

metadata.title: Acute neurotrophic responses to a single bout of blood flow restriction and eccentric overload exercise in healthy older men.
metadata.abstract: Blood flow restriction training (BFRT) combines substantial metabolic stress with low mechanical loading, but its neurotrophic effects remain unclear. This study investigated the acute effects of BFRT and eccentric overload exercise (EOE) on neurotrophic biomarkers in healthy older men. Sixty-three healthy older men (60-78 years) were randomized to BFRT, EOE, or a non-exercising control group. Neurotrophic, metabolic, endothelial, and muscle damage biomarkers were measured before and after exercise. Responses were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA, Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc comparisons, and correlations. Significant time × group interactions were observed for plasma BDNF (p = 0.017, ηp2 = 0.151) and IL-6 (p = 0.001, ηp2 = 0.22), while a marginal time × group interaction was observed for serum IGF-1 (p = 0.050, ηp2 = 0.096). BFRT induced a significant increase in BDNF (mean change = 226.5 pg/mL, p = 0.006), with a greater change compared to CON (p = 0.014). IGF-1 increased significantly from baseline to 1 h post-exercise within the BFRT group (mean change = 29.2 ng/mL, p = 0.005); however, changes did not differ significantly between groups. IL-6 increased significantly following both BFRT (mean change = 8.26 pg/mL, p < 0.001) and EOE (mean change = 3.56 pg/mL, p = 0.013); however, the increase was greater only following BFRT compared to CON (p = 0.001), with no significant difference between BFRT and EOE (p = 0.123). BFRT elicited greater lactate accumulation than EOE and CON, and changes in BDNF correlated with changes in lactate (r = 0.367, p = 0.007). EOE elicited a greater CK increase than CON 48 h post-exercise, whereas syndecan-1 concentrations remained unchanged. Acute BFRT increased circulating BDNF and IGF-1 in healthy older men, and was accompanied by greater lactate accumulation, modest CK elevations, and no detectable increase in syndecan-1. The association between lactate and BDNF suggests that metabolic stress may contribute to the acute peripheral biomarker response; however, the neurological and clinical significance of these transient circulating changes remains to be established.

metadata.title: Structured Physiotherapy Improves Functional Outcomes in Acromegalic Arthropathy After Biochemical Remission: A Prospective Controlled Study.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Musculoskeletal symptoms frequently persist in acromegaly despite biochemical remission, yet the impact of structured physiotherapy on pain, stiffness, and function remains poorly defined. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effects of a standardized knee-focused physiotherapy program in controlled acromegaly and to identify clinical predictors of treatment responsiveness. METHODS: Thirteen patients with acromegaly in remission and 13 age-, gender-, and BMI-matched individuals with primary knee osteoarthritis completed a 15-session physiotherapy program. Outcomes were assessed pre- and post-intervention using the Brief Pain Inventory (BPI) and WOMAC. Minimal clinically significant difference (MCID) thresholds (≥2 for BPI, ≥10 for WOMAC) determined meaningful improvement. Correlation analyses examined associations between clinical variables and Δ scores. RESULTS: Acromegaly patients showed significant improvements in all BPI and WOMAC domains (p<0.001). MCID was achieved by 85% for BPI and 100% for WOMAC Total. Pain and function improved most, whereas stiffness showed limited responsiveness. Compared with osteoarthritis controls, acromegaly patients demonstrated smaller Δ changes; baseline-adjusted analyses (ANCOVA) indicated that this attenuated response was largely explained by greater baseline severity in the control group, whereas the persistently greater stiffness in acromegaly remained significant even after adjustment. BMI correlated positively with improvements in BPI Total (r = 0.63) and BPI Pain Severity (r = 0.69), while adenoma size correlated negatively with both measures (r = -0.57 and -0.60). BMI showed a negative association with WOMAC Total improvement (r = -0.59). Stiffness changes were strongly negatively correlated with pretreatment IGF-1 (r = -0.77). CONCLUSION: Structured physiotherapy yields clinically meaningful improvements in pain and function in acromegaly, while stiffness appears less reversible and more structurally driven. Early musculoskeletal assessment and physiotherapy integration may enhance long-term management.

metadata.title: Menstrual Cycle Phase-Dependent Lower Extremity Loading Patterns in Adolescent Female Athletes: Implications for Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Physically active females experience substantially higher anterior cruciate ligament injury rates than males, and postmenarche adolescent females commonly demonstrate high-risk mechanics. However, whether mechanics fluctuate across the menstrual cycle remains poorly understood in adolescent female athletes. The aim of this study was to examine differences in lower extremity kinematics and kinetics across two menstrual cycle phases (menstruation and mid-luteal) in postmenarchal adolescent female athletes during a dynamic change-of-direction task. It was hypothesized that biomechanical contributors to dynamic knee valgus would differ between phases. METHODS: A controlled laboratory study was conducted. Thirty healthy postmenarchal adolescent female athletes (aged 13-17 years) were tested during menstruation (verified by self-reported active bleeding) and mid-luteal phase (scheduled via calendar-based day counting). Kinematics and kinetics were collected using 3-dimensional motion capture and force plates while participants performed a 45° run-cut task. Peak pelvis, hip, and knee angles and hip and knee moments were extracted during the loading phase for each limb. Linear mixed-effects models tested effects of phase and limb dominance (α = 0.05). RESULTS: Participants were aged 15.6 ± 0.9 years, had a height of 168.8 ± 6.2 cm, and weighed 61.2 ± 7.0 kg, and a majority played soccer (70.0%). Compared with menstruation, the mid-luteal phase demonstrated greater peak anterior pelvic tilt (P = .018) and pelvic rise (P = .038), along with reduced peak knee flexion (P = .009). During menstruation, athletes exhibited greater hip abduction moment (P = .037), hip internal rotation moment (P = .043), knee valgus moment (P = .012), and knee external rotation moment (P = .007). Limb dominance effects were observed for pelvic rise (P < .001) and hip internal rotation moment (P = .047). CONCLUSIONS: Biomechanical contributors linked to dynamic knee valgus differed by menstrual cycle phase in adolescent female athletes during a change-of-direction task. Menstruation was associated with greater coronal- and transverse-plane hip and knee loading, whereas mid-luteal phase was associated with reduced knee flexion and greater pelvic instability. Cycle-synced injury prevention strategies that are individualized and evidence-based may enhance lower extremity stability when knee control appears most challenged. However, while cycle-synced training may not be feasible in all settings, awareness of phase-related vulnerability may inform screening and load management. KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Menstrual cycle phase may contribute to variability in lower extremity biomechanics during change-of-direction tasks in adolescent female athletes.(2)Biomechanical risk factors associated with dynamic knee valgus may differ between menstruation and mid-luteal phases.(3)Consideration of menstrual cycle phase may improve interpretation of biomechanical screening and performance testing.(4)Individualized injury prevention strategies may benefit from awareness of phase-related biomechanical changes. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

metadata.title: Cross-sectional associations of maladaptive sleep-hygiene behaviors with athlete engagement among provincial- and municipal-level athletes in Sichuan, China.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: Maladaptive sleep-hygiene behaviors are potentially modifiable daily practices, yet their relationship with the psychological state that sustains sport involvement remains unclear. This study examined cross-sectional associations among maladaptive sleep-hygiene behaviors (MSHB), multidimensional fatigue, difficulties in emotion regulation, and athlete engagement, including three model-based indirect associations. METHODS: A cross-sectional questionnaire survey was completed by 317 adult athletes recruited from provincial- and municipal-level teams in Sichuan Province, China. Participants represented table tennis, badminton, tennis, basketball, volleyball, and football. The Sleep Hygiene Index, the Chinese Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory, the DERS-16, and the Athlete Engagement Questionnaire were administered. A reflective partial least squares structural equation model was estimated with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Measurement quality, construct differentiation, common-method diagnostics, out-of-sample prediction, demographic adjustment, alternative cross-sectional specifications, and subgroup robustness were evaluated. RESULTS: More frequent MSHB were associated with greater fatigue [β = 0.491, 95% CI (0.408, 0.573)], greater difficulties in emotion regulation [β = 0.178, 95% CI (0.079, 0.274)], and lower athlete engagement [β = -0.264, 95% CI (-0.370, -0.161)]. Fatigue was associated with greater difficulties in emotion regulation [β = 0.588, 95% CI (0.500, 0.673)] and lower engagement [β = -0.325, 95% CI (-0.446, -0.205)]; difficulties in emotion regulation were also associated with lower engagement [β = -0.232, 95% CI (-0.351, -0.108)]. The total indirect association was [β = -0.268, 95% CI (-0.338, -0.204)], and the model explained 47.2% of engagement variance. Demographic adjustment yielded comparable estimates. Reverse-order and parallel specifications fitted the cross-sectional covariance structure equally well. CONCLUSION: Within the sampled setting, more frequent MSHB co-occurred with greater fatigue, more difficulties in emotion regulation, and lower athlete engagement. Fatigue accounted for the largest specific indirect association. The single-occasion self-report design leaves actual sleep disturbance, temporal sequence, and causal effects unresolved.

metadata.title: Cardiac autonomic and hemodynamic responses to two-stage cycling and post-exercise recovery with partial blood flow restriction in young males.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: This study compared acute cardiovascular and cardiac autonomic responses during graded (two-stage) aerobic cycling and subsequent recovery performed with and without partial blood flow restriction (BFR). METHODS: Fifteen young males completed two sessions in a crossover design (control vs. bilateral thigh BFR). Each session included rest, 5 min of cycling at 40% maximal power output (Pmax), 5 min at 60% Pmax, and 10 min of recovery; BFR was released immediately at exercise cessation. ECG and arterial blood pressure were recorded. RR interval, mean arterial blood pressure (MBP), HRV (lnRMSSD, lnSDNN, HF, LF, LF/HF), and composite indices of cardiac sympathetic and parasympathetic activity (SNS, PNS) were derived from 3-min segments at rest, exercise, and recovery. Heart rate recovery at 30, 60, and 120 s after exercise cessation (HRR30, HRR60, HRR120) was calculated. Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA tested condition, time, and interaction. RESULTS: Time × condition interactions were observed for RR interval (p=0.015) and MBP (p=0.003), indicating altered hemodynamic kinetics under BFR, primarily during recovery. HRV indices showed no time × condition interactions; however, BFR produced lower lnRMSSD, lnSDNN, HF, and PNS and higher SNS than control (all p<0.05), whereas LF and LF/HF were unchanged. HRR30 (p=0.040), HRR60 (p<0.001), and HRR120 (p=0.010) were attenuated under BFR. CONCLUSIONS: BFR modifies cardiovascular regulation during two-stage cycling and recovery and induces sustained autonomic shifts toward reduced parasympathetic and increased sympathetic modulation, largely independent of exercise intensity. Altered recovery kinetics following cuff release highlight the importance of careful monitoring during the recovery phase when applying BFR.

metadata.title: The Sonographic Muscle Injury Classification in Soccer: proposal for an ultrasound-based muscle injury classification.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To propose a novel ultrasound-based classification system for muscle injuries in soccer players, termed the Sonographic Muscle Injury Classification in Soccer (SOMICS), and to evaluate its association, ordinal consistency, and agreement with the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC). MATERIALS AND METHODS: This was a cross-sectional observational study including 51 adolescent male soccer players (11-19 years of age) with suspected acute myotendinous injuries. All athletes underwent ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) within 24 h after injury. Four experienced radiologists, working independently, reviewed the images. RESULTS: Interobserver agreement was substantial for ultrasound (κ = 0.65) and MRI (κ = 0.70). A strong ordinal correlation was observed between SOMICS and BAMIC categories (ρ = 0.80; p < 0.001), with a statistically significant association (χ2 = 52.53; p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: The SOMICS demonstrated significant association, ordinal consistency, and substantial agreement with the BAMIC for severity stratification of muscle injuries. Although not intended to replace MRI-based classifications for prognostic decision-making, the SOMICS provides a structured, reproducible ultrasound-based approach that may be useful in clinical settings where MRI is not readily available or as a first-line imaging tool.

metadata.title: Transient ST-T Changes During Submaximal Exercise Revealing Anomalous Right Coronary Artery Origin in an Asymptomatic Athlete.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Anomalous aortic origin of a coronary artery is a recognised structural cause of sudden cardiac death in athletes younger than 35 years. Most affected individuals are asymptomatic prior to cardiac events, and resting and exercise electrocardiography (ECG) findings are frequently normal or non-specific, limiting the effectiveness of preparticipation screening. CASE SUMMARY: We report a case of a 22-year-old asymptomatic athlete in whom preparticipation screening revealed transient ST-segment depression and T-wave inversions during submaximal exercise and recovery, whereas findings at peak exercise remained normal. Point-of-care echocardiography performed by a sports medicine specialist raised suspicion of an anomalous origin of the right coronary artery from the left aortic sinus of Valsalva, which was subsequently confirmed by computed tomography coronary angiography. High-risk anatomical features included an acute ostial angle and an interarterial course of the right coronary artery. Functional testing with exercise myocardial stress scintigraphy showed no inducible perfusion defect. Following multidisciplinary consultation, a conservative management strategy with activity modification and close follow-up was adopted. DISCUSSION: This case highlights the potential clinical significance of transient ST-T abnormalities occurring during submaximal exercise and recovery, even in the absence of symptoms or abnormalities at peak workload. In this patient, recognition of this reproducible but non-specific ECG pattern prompted further structural evaluation leading to the diagnosis of AAOCA. It also underscores the limitations of current guidelines in managing asymptomatic athletes with high-risk coronary anatomy but without evidence of inducible ischaemia, supporting the need for individualised decision-making.

metadata.title: Imaging of acute sports injuries of the shoulder girdle.
metadata.abstract: Acute injuries of the shoulder girdle commonly result from sports activities and lead to imaging studies. Radiologists who interpret these studies should be familiar with traumatic mechanisms and the imaging manifestations of glenohumeral dislocation, acromioclavicular sprain, rotator cuff tear, labral tear, osseous contusion or fracture, and myotendinous strain. Imaging findings are crucial for making accurate diagnoses, grading the severity of injuries, guiding treatment plans, and managing the athletes' expectations for rehabilitation and return to sport. In this review article, we address common and uncommon injuries in both young and mature athletes. Focusing on magnetic resonance imaging, we provide examples of classic injuries and discuss pitfalls that challenge diagnostic interpretation.

metadata.title: Effects of muscle length and age on neuromuscular responses to maximal eccentric contractions of the plantar flexors.
metadata.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Eccentric contractions induce greater neuromuscular impairment and muscle damage than concentric contractions. Muscle length is a key modulator of these responses, yet the combined effects of eccentric contractions and muscle length on neuromuscular function in older adults remain unclear. We investigated acute and delayed neuromuscular responses to eccentric plantar flexor contractions performed at different muscle lengths in young and older adults. METHODS: Twenty-four young and 26 older adults performed 10 sets of 10 maximal eccentric plantar flexor contractions at either short (30°-0° plantar flexion) or long (0°-30° dorsiflexion) muscle lengths (12 young and 13 older adults per condition). Maximal voluntary isometric contraction, voluntary activation, and evoked responses (100 Hz and 10 Hz doublets) were measured before, immediately after, and 1, 24, and 48 h post-exercise. Changes were compared between groups and conditions. RESULTS: Despite similar torque-time integrals between young and older adults within the same muscle length condition, a muscle length effect was only found in young adults, with a greater (p = 0.021) MVIC decrease at long (-33.6 ± 13.2%) than short lengths (-8.4 ± 15.7%). Older adults showed similar reductions across conditions (≈ - 14-21%). Voluntary activation decreased only at long lengths, with no age difference. Evoked responses showed an age effect (p = 0.032), and the 10/100 Hz ratio decreased only in young after long muscle lengths. Neuromuscular function returned to baseline within 24 h indicating no evidence of severe alteration, although muscle soreness remained elevated at 48 h. CONCLUSION: Long muscle length eccentric contractions induced greater force loss in young but not older adults, with no evidence of prolonged functional impairment in healthy, physically active older adults.

metadata.title: Bilateral erector spinae and biceps femoris co-activation following unilateral hamstring injury in young sprinters.
metadata.abstract: This study compared coactivation and strength of the erector spinae (ES) and biceps femoris long head (BFLH) during isometric knee flexion and trunk extension in sprinters with a recent BFLH injury. Twenty-four sprinters with grade 2 BFLH injury and 21 controls performed prone trunk extension and knee flexion maximal voluntary contractions (MVCs) at 90° and 0° knee flexion. Torque and surface electromyography (EMG) of the ES and BFLH were recorded bilaterally and normalized to MVCs during 30° trunk extension and 0° knee flexion, respectively. Previously injured athletes showed a greater co-contraction index (CCI) during knee flexion at 0° and 90° than controls (p < 0.001), with higher ES activation (32.52 ± 17.08 to 47.72 ± 17.83% MVC) than the uninjured group (21.56 ± 14.52 to 44.68 ± 18.02% MVC; p < 0.05). No group differences were found in normalized BFLH EMG, CCI during trunk extension, or absolute knee flexion or trunk extension strength (p > 0.05). Previously injured sprinters showed larger between-limb knee flexion strength asymmetries (>10%, p < 0.01), which were absent in controls. This paraspinal overactivation and increased trunk-hamstring co-contraction after BFLH injury suggest that lumbopelvic control exercises may be beneficial for preventing BFLH re-injury.

metadata.title: Advanced Footwear Technology in Distance Running: What We Know, What We Don't Know, and Future Directions.
metadata.abstract: Over the past decade, running shoes have undergone substantial innovation with the emergence of Advanced Footwear Technology (AFT). Shoes with AFT are typically characterized by highly compliant (deformable) and resilient (high energy return) midsole foams, embedded curved stiffening elements, low mass, and a rockered longitudinal geometry. This expert statement aims to synthesize established knowledge, remaining uncertainties and key directions for future research on AFT in middle- and long-distance running. Current literature demonstrates robust improvements in running economy and performance with AFT, with reported metabolic savings of approximately 2%-4%, and corresponding performance improvements of 1%-3%. These benefits likely arise from a combination of "acute" and possibly "long-term" mechanisms. Proposed acute mechanisms include decreased muscle force production due to higher positive work from energy-returning foams, lower muscle force production to accommodate mechanical running demands due to compliant midsoles, and improved mechanical efficiency associated with greater longitudinal bending stiffness and curved geometry. Importantly, AFT features have a synergistic effect, with the relative importance of each mechanism differing depending on the context. Emerging evidence also suggests potential reductions in muscle damage/inflammation and soreness, which could support better physiological resilience, and higher training volumes/quality. From a biomechanical injury risk perspective, AFT can redistribute loading, potentially increasing metatarsal and tarsal stress while reducing tibia and possibly Achilles tendon loading. However, injury risk associated with AFT use remains equivocal, with limited high-quality data. Notably, substantial inter-individual variability has been observed, influencing both running economy and potential injury risk although the determinants of this variability remain unclear.

metadata.title: Exploring the Impact of Ovarian Hormones on Cortical Drive and Quadriceps Performance in Uninjured Female Athletes.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Ovarian hormones fluctuate across the menstrual cycle (MC) and differ between oral contraceptive (OC) users and naturally menstruating (NM) individuals. Hormones may affect cortical drive to peripheral muscles through excitatory effects of estradiol and inhibitory effects of progesterone on the central nervous system. The impact of hormones on cortical drive is poorly understood. This study aimed to (1) determine the effects of MC phase and OC use on cortical drive and quadriceps performance and (2) determine the relationship between ovarian hormones and these outcomes. We hypothesized that cortical drive will differ between MC phases in NM individuals but not in OC users. Cortical drive will be positively associated with circulating estradiol. METHODS: Fourteen NM individuals and 11 OC users completed two time points (high hormone: NM mid-luteal, OC active pill and low hormone: NM early follicular, OC placebo). Hormone concentrations were quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Quadriceps performance (isometric peak torque [PTISOM] and rate of torque development) was measured using an isokinetic dynamometer. Corticospinal excitability and intracortical excitability (short-interval intracortical inhibition [SICI] and intracortical facilitation) were assessed using transcranial magnetic stimulation. Linear mixed-effect models were used to examine hormone status, phase, and interaction effects. Linear regression determined associations between hormones, cortical drive, and strength. RESULTS: There were no significant main effects or interactions for any cortical drive measure. There was a phase by hormone status interaction on the rate of torque development from 0 to 100 ms (RTD100), with a greater RTD100 at the high hormone phase than at the low hormone phase in the NM group but no difference between time points in the OC group. There was a main effect of phase on PTISOM, with a greater PTISOM at the low hormone phase regardless of hormone status. SICI was negatively associated with estradiol. RTD100 was positively associated with progesterone and moderated by hormone status. CONCLUSIONS: MC phase did not impact cortical drive but did impact quadriceps performance. There were between-phase differences in speed of contraction among NM individuals but not among OC users. A higher progesterone level was associated with faster speed of contraction, especially among NM participants. KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Corticospinal and intracortical excitability did not differ by menstrual cycle (MC) phase or oral contraceptive (OC) use.(2)Quadriceps rate of torque development was associated with progesterone concentration and varied across the MC, suggesting hormone expression influenced the rate of torque development (RTD) (speed of contraction).(3)The influence of endogenous ovarian hormones on RTD (speed of contraction) differed between OC users and naturally menstruating individuals. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: II.

metadata.title: Shoulder Instability Pediatric Management of Shoulder Instability in the Pediatric Athlete: A Contemporary Review of Current Evidence.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Shoulder instability in pediatric and adolescent athletes is increasingly common and clinically complex due to early sport specialization and high-demand participation. This review aims to inform clinical decision-making by synthesizing contemporary evidence on injury patterns, diagnostic techniques, treatment options, and associated outcomes when faced with treating pediatric athletes. RECENT FINDINGS: Unique anatomic and developmental features specific to the pediatric population including capsular elasticity, collagen composition, open physes, and evolving glenoid and humeral morphology contribute to age-specific injury patterns and influence treatment outcomes. Younger children more frequently sustain atypical soft-tissue lesions, while adolescents experience markedly higher recurrence risk with rates of 44-77% following nonoperative management. Adolescents also develop off-track Hill-Sachs lesions more frequently than adults (24.4% vs. 3.3%), reflecting differences in immature bone mechanics. Diagnosis requires thorough history, physical examination, assessment of social and socioeconomic factors, and advanced imaging. Arthroscopic Bankart repair remains the most common surgical intervention and yields high return to sport rates (75-90%), though recurrence in pediatric patients (15-50%) substantially exceeds adult rates. Remplissage reduces recurrence in adolescents with off-track lesions, and bone augmentation procedures such as the Latarjet demonstrate lower recurrence (3-8%) in patients with significant glenoid bone loss or failed prior stabilization. Long-term outcomes in skeletally immature patients and alternative bone block procedures remain incompletely studied. Management requires individualized risk stratification based on adherence, skeletal maturity, sport demands, bone loss, lesion morphology and patient history and adherence. Although surgical stabilization provides favorable functional outcomes and high return to sport rates, recurrence remains a significant concern in younger and collision-sport athletes.

metadata.title: Facilitators and Barriers to Treatment Access and Use in Black Individuals With Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: A Qualitative Study.
metadata.abstract: CONTEXT: Individuals with anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury are at high risk of knee osteoarthritis. Black individuals with osteoarthritis have worse pain and disability than White individuals. Racial disparities in ACL treatment use (ACL reconstruction and physical therapy) may contribute to disparities in long-term osteoarthritis-related disability. However, factors influencing ACL injury disparities are unknown. We explored facilitators and barriers to treatment access and use in Black individuals with ACL injury. DESIGN: Qualitative (semistructured interviews). METHODS: We included Black or African American individuals who self-reported ACL injury up to 5 years prior to recruitment, no longer seeking care for the injury, and 16-50 years old. We conducted one-on-one semistructured interviews and topics included facilitators and barriers to care, perceived communication, medical trust, and perceived discrimination. We used a reflexive thematic analysis approach to analyze the interviews. RESULTS: We included 10 participants (age 21-49 y, 8 women). We generated 4 themes: (1) path to diagnosis, (2) patient approach to treatment, (3) patient-provider interactions, and (4) life demands. ACL injury recovery was often complex with frustrations particularly common during the diagnosis process due to lack of an accurate diagnosis and poor communication on next steps. Participants took various approaches to treatment use including active, passive, and more autonomous approaches. Family obligations and transportation barriers posed challenges to accessing treatment. Lack of health insurance was a barrier affecting multiple aspects of recovery. Participants often desired shared decision making. Several types of perceived discrimination were discussed including race, gender, insurance, and weight. Facilitators were often related to positive communication or athletic program resources. CONCLUSION: Facilitators included shared decision making, provider empathy and encouragement, and athletic program resources. Barriers included a lack of listening to patients' concerns, lack of health insurance, transportation challenges, and perceived discrimination.

metadata.title: A wearable vibroarthrography system with PID-controlled negative-pressure suction and synchronized posture estimation.
metadata.abstract: BackgroundVibroarthrography (VAG) is a non-invasive technique for evaluating joint health through acoustic signals generated during movement. However, reliable signal acquisition during dynamic activities remains challenging due to sensor displacement, motion artifacts, and inconsistent skin contact.ObjectiveThis study proposes an advanced wearable VAG system integrating PID-controlled negative-pressure suction and real-time posture estimation to improve signal stability and enhance the assessment of knee joint mechanics during movement.MethodsThe proposed system combines a wearable acoustic sensing module with a vacuum-assisted suction cup and a PID controller that consistently maintains sensor adhesion. Real-time posture estimation is achieved using MediaPipe Pose, which computes knee flexion angles. VAG signals and kinematic data are synchronously acquired during OKC and CKC exercises for integrated analysis.ResultsIn this single-subject pilot test, the system achieved stable sensor attachment and repeatable vibroacoustic recordings throughout dynamic movements. Distinguishable frequency-domain characteristics were observed at relevant knee flexion angles, including approximately 30°, 63°, and 129°.ConclusionsThis pilot feasibility study demonstrates that the proposed wearable VAG platform can achieve stable acquisition of synchronized vibroacoustic and kinematic signals during dynamic knee movement in a single subject. These preliminary findings suggest potential future applications in osteoarthritis screening, rehabilitation assessment, and ambulatory monitoring, pending validation in larger, statistically powered cohorts.

metadata.title: Combined effects of photobiomodulation and platelet-rich plasma on healing of acute Achilles tendon injuries in rats.
metadata.abstract: Tendon injuries are challenging to treat due to limited intrinsic healing, and although photobiomodulation (PBM) and platelet-rich plasma (PRP) show therapeutic potential, their combined effects remain unclear. This study evaluated the individual and combined efficacy of PBM and PRP on Achilles tendon repair in rats. A total of 144 rats were assigned to six groups and treated with PBM, PRP, or combined PBM + PRP therapy; tissues were collected at 1 and 8 weeks for biochemical and histological assessment. Both PBM and PRP reduced IL-1β and TNF-α levels and improved collagen organization, while the combined therapy produced the most pronounced anti-inflammatory response and structural recovery. Notably, PBM + PRP significantly enhanced and prolonged PDGF-BB expression compared with either treatment alone. These findings demonstrate that PBM and PRP each promote tendon healing, but their combination yields superior therapeutic benefits through amplified modulation of inflammatory and regenerative pathways, highlighting their potential as an improved therapeutic strategy.

metadata.title: UEFA consensus guidelines on anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in Women's football - part one: risk factors and prevention.
metadata.abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are among the most burdensome injuries in women's football, carrying significant consequences for players and the football community. To develop practical, evidence-based guidelines for ACL injury prevention, UEFA convened a multidisciplinary expert panel of 31 doctors, sports scientists, physiotherapists, and a player. Using the RAND-UCLA Appropriateness Method, 101 evidence statements were synthesised from existing literature and subjected to a modified Delphi process with three rounds of confidential voting. Consensus was reached on 88 statements. Through online and in-person discussions, this evidence was integrated with expert and clinical and practical judgement to produce actionable recommendations tailored to women's football. The guidelines conclude that ACL injuries in women's football typically occur in non-contact situations during high-intensity movements such as cutting, pressing, or landing, and may be influenced by a combination of modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors. Proposed modifiable factors include deficits in neuromuscular control, strength, and movement quality, which can be addressed through multicomponent prevention strategies. These programmes were identified as the most effective, incorporating plyometric, strength, and proximal control exercises performed two to three times per week for 15 to 20 minutes, with evidence showing they can reduce non-contact ACL injuries when adherence is high. Successful implementation requires context-specific tailoring, embedding programmes into routine training, and addressing barriers such as limited resources, time constraints, and lack of coach education. The guidelines recommend enhancing buy-in through co-creation with coaches and players, integrating prevention into existing practice, and strengthening organisational and policy support to sustain long-term adoption.

metadata.title: Ask the experts: a practitioner-centred approach to resilience in emergency medical services.
metadata.abstract: Background: Resilience in high-stress occupations is commonly framed as a trait, an outcome, or the absence of psychopathology. None of these framings captures what practitioners in emergency medical services actually do, and interventions built on trait-based models have produced weak or inconsistent effects.Objective: This study argues that frontline resilience in emergency medical services is better understood as a domain-specific expert skill, and that work mode - a deliberately entered state, akin to an athlete's game face, in which the demands of the task rather than the emotional force of the scene govern functioning - is its central empirical signature. The aims were to identify factors that intensify traumatic impact, characterise the strategies practitioners use to maintain functioning, and explore systemic and relational barriers that constrain coping.Method: Twenty Queensland Ambulance Service paramedics and dispatchers (tenure 2-38 years) participated in semi-structured interviews, analysed via reflexive thematic analysis.Results: Three intensifiers of traumatic impact (unpredictability, moral weight, personal threat) defined the operational demands against which resilience was enacted. Three coping themes (baseline buffers, work mode, social scaffolding) described the architecture of sustained functioning. Work mode exhibited the defining features of skilled performance: domain specificity, a phased temporal structure (preparation, containment, recovery), and a developmental trajectory from effortful to automatic execution. Two further themes (organisational distrust, the outsider gap) described the systemic and relational conditions that constrain coping.Conclusions: Treating resilience as expertise shifts the field from descriptive stressor-outcome accounts towards assessable, trainable capacities, and exposes the limitations of trait-based self-report measures that cannot distinguish genuine resilience from unsustainable stoicism.

metadata.title: Running-based rehabilitation does not improve muscle function after volumetric muscle loss despite improving hindlimb weight-bearing asymmetry in mice.
metadata.abstract: Volumetric muscle loss (VML) is a traumatic skeletal muscle injury characterized by chronic functional impairments in the affected muscle and adjacent uninjured bone. Rehabilitative strategies aimed at restoring limb function following VML, including voluntary running, have shown limited efficacy and in some cases have been detrimental. One potential explanation is disproportional loading of the uninjured contralateral limb during running, but evaluation of unilateral weight-bearing following VML has not been explored. This study was designed to evaluate if the limited response to rehabilitation following VML could be explained by limb loading asymmetry. Twelve-week-old C57Bl/6J mice (n = 24; equal males/females) were randomized to three groups: Naïve-Run, VML, and VML-Run. Two weeks post-VML, mice in running groups were provided free access to wheels for 6 weeks. Weight-bearing asymmetry was assessed before injury and biweekly thereafter. Terminally at ∼20 weeks of age, in vivo muscle function was evaluated, and muscles and bones were saved for analyses. Prior to injury, no difference in weight-bearing asymmetry was observed across groups. VML-injured mice exhibited similar weight-bearing asymmetries prior to running. Following 6 weeks of running, VML-Run mice regained weight-bearing symmetry comparable to Naïve-Run. Despite this, remaining muscle function remained persistently impaired following VML injury. Collectively this works suggests that voluntary running promotes favourable weight-bearing adaptations following VML, but does not improve muscle function or the mechanical properties of the adjacent bone.
